entries.title: Trump Announces Efforts to Tamp Down Surging Diesel Prices
entries.summary: The White House has searched for ways to lower prices for farmers who are hit with high costs at the peak of harvest season.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump announced several measures to lower diesel prices during a rally in Nebraska on Monday, looking to address a major concern for rural voters a month before the midterms.

Farmers and ranchers in the state and in other battleground states are frustrated with high diesel prices at the peak of harvest season. Diesel fuel prices have reached record high prices due to the ongoing war with Iran and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries. The increase has angered farmers and added to persistent inflation that threatens the GOP's hold on Congress.

Trump announced and signed the orders on stage to make more red-dyed diesel readily available. That diesel is tax-exempt and used in farming, construction and other industries. Politico reported that the package also includes a Treasury Department review of certain diesel taxes and would also urge states to waive some fuel taxes, but the immediate details aren’t clear.

Diesel is one of the several major issues causing Republicans trouble for farmers this year. Trump’s recent moves to import hundreds of thousands of tons of beef from Brazil and Argentina, and a reignited trade war with Canada, have turned one-safe races in states Trump won by large margins into competitive ones.

Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins teased the move earlier on Monday, saying that the Trump administration and the Department of Agriculture were prioritizing short-term relief for farmers at the pump and that 10 states are taking action to lower prices as well.

“In just the last few days we’ve seen the cost of a gallon of diesel go down about 15 cents,” Rollins said on Fox News. “We have more to do.”

Trump had mulled a diesel export ban but ultimately decided against it after pushback from the oil industry and Energy Secretary Chris Wright, who warned it would negatively impact allies and encourage producers to cut production in response.

The decision on an export ban came after the Group of Seven countries agreed Thursday to release up to 100 million barrels of crude and diesel from emergency stockpiles over four months. The deal includes what the G7 statement called "a front-loaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days."

entries.title: Supreme Court Rejects a Last-Ditch Effort to Block the Paramount-Warner Merger
entries.summary: The deal for Paramount to acquire Warner Bros. closes Tuesday.
entries.content:
The Supreme Court denied a last-minute bid by streaming subscribers seeking to block Paramount Skydance’s $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. just hours before the megamerger was expected to close on Tuesday.

Monday’s longshot emergency application, addressed to Justice Elena Kagan, sought to keep the companies separate while the court considers reviewing a challenge filed by a group of Paramount subscribers. Without the high court’s intervention, the merger is expected to continue, solidifying the two film studios — as well as CNN, CBS News, TBS, HGTV, Paramount+ and HBO — under one company.

“Closing will not merely change a stock ledger,” the applicants wrote in their request. “Once independent pricing, programming, release, newsroom, technology, employment and investment decisions are centralized, later relief cannot restore the period of competition that was lost.”

Within a matter of hours, Kagan denied the emergency appeal without comment.

The lawsuit, initially filed in April, alleged that the acquisition would eliminate competition between businesses that currently vie for consumers’ money and attention. In their Monday filing, the consumers pleaded with the Supreme Court to review their case, arguing that U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin overlooked evidence already in the record, including Paramount’s own plans to lay off employees.

Lower courts had already tossed other efforts by consumers to slow the deal. Last week, Martinez-Olguin approved a settlement agreement between Paramount, the Writers Guild of America and 12 states challenging the acquisition, resolving the monthslong deadlock over the merger.

In exchange for letting the deal move forward, Paramount Skydance must spend at least $1.5 billion domestically to produce a minimum of 30 film releases each year. The settlement also includes protections for editorial independence at CNN and CBS News and creates safeguards against writer layoffs.

Lina Khan, the Federal Trade Commission chair under President Joe Biden, said that such fail-safes in high-stakes antitrust cases often fall short of protecting the markets.

“Behavioral remedies routinely fail, and the stakes here are particularly high given that a strong democracy requires open markets for sound journalism and creative expression,” she wrote on X last month.

According to a Paramount filing, layoffs will soon hit workers in Hollywood. The company is mostly looking at nonunion corporate and desk jobs where duties overlap, but officials said they also plan to cut production for some film and television titles.

The newly merged company will be named Skydance, led by David Ellison alongside co-CEO Ynon Kreiz. Paramount has already projected more than $6 billion in savings and approximately $79 billion in net debt, while the younger Ellison has argued that combining streaming operations would strengthen competition with Netflix.

Kriez said Monday that the merger will make Skydance the leader in the global media market by building “the most technologically capable media company” and “capitalizing on our scale, assets and global reach.”

The transaction also carries political stakes: President Donald Trump, who shares close ties with the Ellison family, has publicly demanded new ownership for CNN, a network he frequently assails for critical coverage. Trump recently barred CNN reporters from accessing the White House.

"I think the people that have run CNN for the last long period of time are a disgrace. I think it's imperative that CNN be sold,” Trump told reporters in December. “I don't think the people that are running that company right now and running CNN — which is a very dishonest group of people — I don't think that should be allowed to continue."

Trump’s Justice Department closed its merger investigation in June, concluding that the deal was “unlikely to harm” competition or consumers.

Paramount announced Monday that CNN chief Mark Thompson would remain in charge of the network as the company prepares to bring it under the same ownership as CBS News.

entries.title: Trump Approves Firing Squad Execution for Fort Hood Shooter
entries.summary: The U.S. military hasn't carried out the death penalty since 1961.
entries.content:
By Jonathan J. Cooper

President Donald Trump has approved the execution by firing squad of Army Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan for the 2009 shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas.

The U.S. military has not carried out the death penalty since 1961. The Army secretary will decide a time and place for the execution, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell wrote in a post on X.

“Judgement day for Hasan has finally come,” Parnell wrote.

Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, walked into a medical building where soldiers were getting medical checkups, shouted “Allahu akbar” — Arabic for “God is great!” — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. Thirteen people were killed and more than 30 injured.

He said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims and made almost no effort to defend himself at trial. He told jurors that evidence would show he was the shooter and described himself as a soldier who had “switched sides.”

Trump’s approval triggers a series of procedural steps toward carrying out the execution, but Hasan could put them on hold — potentially for years — with a habeas corpus appeal in the civilian federal court system, according to an article published in May in the magazine Army Lawyer.

Death sentences are extremely rare in the military justice system, and executions even rarer. Four men, including Hasan, are currently on the military's death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. President George W. Bush approved the execution Army Spc. Ronald Gray in 2008 but it was put on hold by a judge and he remains at Leavenworth.

The last man executed in the military system was Pvt. John Bennett, hanged in 1961 for raping an 11-year-old girl.

Trump approved the firing squad execution days after a failed attempt to execute Christa Pike by lethal injection pushed Tennessee’s governor to halt further executions this year and order an independent review.

Trump resumed the federal death penalty after an informal moratorium during previous administrations. The federal government executed 13 people between 2020 and early 2021, contributing to making Trump the most prolific execution president in over 130 years.

Asked whether the botched execution in Tennessee would lead him to seek changes to capital punishment, Trump said it was “an interesting situation.”

“It shouldn’t be very difficult,” Trump said of carrying out lethal injections.

entries.title: Jayden Daniels Is on Track to Return Sunday Against the Giants
entries.summary: Backup quarterback Marcus Mariota is out with a knee injury, but guard Sam Cosmi, safety Nick Cross and running back Rachaad White will all be back on the field.
entries.content:
After missing the past two games, quarterback Jayden Daniels is expected to return to the lineup this Sunday against the Giants.

“The goal is for [Daniels] to have a full week of practice and start on Sunday,” head coach Dan Quinn said Monday.

Daniels will be joined by several fellow returning injured players: right guard Sam Cosmi, safety Nick Cross and running back Rachaad White.

Receiver Jaylin Lane will miss the rest of the season after fracturing his foot Sunday against the Colts in London. Quarterback Marcus Mariota (knee) and defensive end Charles Omenihu (groin) were also injured on Sunday, but their timeline for returning is still up in the air.

Daniels has missed the past two games after dislocating his left elbow for the second time in 10 months. The third-year quarterback went to London with the team and practiced, but didn’t dress in the loss to the Colts.

Third-string quarterback Athan Kaliakmanis made his NFL debut on Sunday in Washington’s 30-13 loss after Mariota injured his knee, and performed well given the circumstances. Kaliakmanis completed 15 of his 33 passes for 186 yards with a touchdown and interception. Despite his inexperience, Kaliakmanis wasn’t afraid to take shots downfield. He became the only quarterback this season to throw more than six passes of 30 yards-plus. His first career touchdown pass was a perfectly placed 47-yard strike to Treylon Burks.

Quinn said that three players currently on injured reserve — cornerback Trey Amos (ankle), running back Jeremy McNichols (quad) and defensive lineman Deatrich Wise (quad) — will be evaluated this week to see if they're ready to return to play.

entries.title: All-DMV High School Volleyball Players of Week 5
entries.summary: This week’s group features a senior outside hitter from Eleanor Roosevelt and setters from Coolidge and Thomas Jefferson.
entries.content:
This story is part of The Washington Sun’s All-DMV coverage. All-DMV is a new collaboration between The Sun, Fox 5 DC, NBC4 Washington and WTOP News, aimed at covering the D.C. area’s best high school athletes. You can find past players of the week and more information about All-DMV here.

Between a freshman setter from D.C. to a senior captain outside hitter from Prince George’s County, this week’s crop of All-DMV volleyball Players of the Week showcase the depth of talent in the area — regardless of age or position. Here’s who stood out the most in Week 5:

Marley DeGeneste, Freshman, Setter, Coolidge

Coolidge picked up two commanding wins last week, and their freshman setter was a big reason why. DeGeneste dominated from behind the service line for the Colts — she logged double-digit service aces in 2-0 victories over Anacostia and Phelps. DeGeneste scored 13 service aces in the latter matchup, the team’s eighth victory of the season.

Despite just picking up volleyball recently, DeGeneste has quickly found her footing with the sport and excelled at the setter position, Coolidge coach Clarke Jamison said.

“She’s really attached to the setter position so effortlessly and flawlessly,” Jamison said. “She’s amazing at getting her feet to the ball, really setting her hips to set that ball wherever she’s looking to set it.”

Iris Jin, Junior, Setter, Thomas Jefferson

Midway through Thomas Jefferson’s matchup against Edison last week, coach Tim Kao scribbled a message on his clipboard to quietly alert his bench of an incoming milestone. “She’s down to one,” Kao remembers whispering to his players. “The kids were ready with signs and balloons and posters.”

Moments later, with a perfectly placed pass to set up a Colonials kill, Jin recorded her 1,000th career assist for the Alexandria program. She finished with 18 assists on the evening in the eventual 3-0 sweep and also logged 30 assists in a win over Mount Vernon two days earlier.

Serayah Williams, Senior, Outside Hitter, Eleanor Roosevelt

With several key players out due to injury, the Raiders leaned on Williams heavily to preserve their unbeaten streak. The senior outside hitter responded by totalling 16 kills and six service aces in a four-set win over county rival Flowers on the road last Wednesday. With Williams, a second-year captain, leading the charge, coach Michelle Blacks’ team has dropped just one set so far this season.

“Serayah has shown incredible leadership this year,” Blacks said. “It’s her last season, she wants to go out with a bang. … She’s a powerhouse right now.”

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: Fare Warning
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Oct. 6, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: A floated fare increase, Ovipalooza and DMV homes with a view.

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 9/10. A slightly cool but absolutely awesome autumn day. We can soak it in and enjoy as we look forward to at least a few more sunny days ahead too! Full forecast from Capital Weather.

THE LATEST

Inflation in the station: WMATA is proposing an 11.1% fare increase to keep pace with inflation, The Washington Sun’s Justice Covert reports.

The transit authority’s Finance and Capital Committee will discuss the proposal at a Thursday meeting. It would raise the cost of riding Metro to between $2.50 and $7.50 starting in fiscal year 2028, up from the current $2.25 to $6.75 range.

The move is expected to generate $40 million to $45 million in revenue, but also result in 8 million fewer trips. Fares were last hiked in 2024 by 12.5%. The proposed increase would apply to all fares, including Metro Access.

“It’s understandable given inflation,” said Stewart Schwartz, executive director of the Coalition for Smarter Growth, pointing to higher fuel costs. “It’s, overall, a relatively modest increase.”

The fare increase is just one reform WMATA is proposing. Another is a universal youth fare program that would offer all children ages 5 to 18 who live in the DMV free rides on the Metrobus and Metrorail — WMATA’s proposal said that it would cost $7 million and add 900,000 trips.

Not everyone is convinced that initiative and other reforms go far enough to offset the increase.

“At a time when bus ridership is down and Metro is cracking down on fare evaders, higher fares are a big turn off for riders, especially people on fixed incomes,” Alex Baca, D.C. policy director at GGWash, said in a statement shared with The Sun. “As budget season approaches, we’re hopeful that Metro will work with local jurisdictions to find a funding solution that doesn’t hurt the hundreds of thousands of people across our region who rely on transit.”

The committee will not take any action on the proposal on Thursday. WMATA officials recommend the Metro Board of Directors schedule a public hearing to collect feedback before implementing the changes.





DEEP DIVE

Get ready for six months of Ovipalooza. 

By announcing he will retire at the end of this Washington Capitals season, superstar Alexander Ovechkin has ensured this 2026-27 NHL campaign — beginning with Wednesday night’s Capitals home opener at Capital One Arena — will serve as one long farewell tour for the league’s all-time leading goal-scorer. Monday’s announcement was unsurprising — Ovechkin, 41, has seen his ice time and production decline in recent years — but it still landed like a high-stick to the teeth, particularly here in Washington, where Ovechkin has spent the entirety of his 22-year NHL career.

Twenty-five years ago this summer, another iconic athlete from this region — who also wore uniform No. 8 and spent his entire career on one team — launched a similar farewell tour. Baltimore Orioles legend Cal Ripken Jr. was feted by every team in the league in his final stop at each stadium, culminating in a memorable send-off at Camden Yards.

But there is one major difference between Ripken and Ovechkin: While the former was universally beloved across the country, Ovechkin’s association with Russia's Vladimir Putin, for whom he has been a frequent and public supporter, will almost certainly complicate the atmosphere in each road city when Ovipalooza comes to town.

The Capitals, meanwhile, are planning to celebrate the “Great 8” on the eighth of each month this season — but even here the reaction might be mixed, as the group D.C. Stands With Ukraine plans to protest Ovechkin’s ties to Putin before Wednesday night’s home opener, saying, “We’ll be there to send a clear message to Ovechkin, the Capitals, their sponsors and the venue: support for mass murderers has consequences.”





FROM THE DISTRICT

Democracy, delivered. Make sure to check your mailbox, because D.C. residents should start receiving their ballots for the November election in the mail this week. If you’re really gunning to do your civic duty early, 55 ballot drop boxes will open across D.C. on Oct. 9 at 11 a.m. and will remain accessible until the polls close on Nov. 3 at 8 p.m. All registered voters will get a ballot mailed to them, but if for some reason you don’t get one by Oct. 30, plan to vote in person.

Food insecurity throughout the region has increased as access to SNAP and Medicaid benefits became limited through the Trump-backed "one big, beautiful bill," The Sun’s Shamira Muhammad reports — and local organizations are stepping in to help.

After nixing the idea of a second Metro station at the new Commanders stadium, today the D.C. Council will vote on whether to provide WMATA with $300 million for improvements at the existing Stadium-Armory station, and $50 million for the first phase of the “Gold Line” bus system running along H Street between the stadium and Union Station.

A Dream Home Makeover for the Nats? Mayor Muriel Bowser has introduced a bill to finance a planned $400 million renovation of 18-year-old Nationals Park to turn it into a “state-of-the-art venue that competes with newer facilities.” The project will be paid for by an existing tax on businesses, as well as sales taxes on products sold in the stadium itself.

D.C.’s tour guides tell The Washington Post that bookings have tanked this year by as much as 70%, as many of the District’s iconic sites are under renovation or closed.





HOMES WITH A VIEW

00C4DEEB-5CCB-42E9-86DE-428B8F9CE7E4.png (1535x1025, AR: 1.50)
Aren’t we all looking for an escape sometimes? A roof deck might be just the answer, and Michele Lerner has rounded up homes around the DMV with a private or shared roof deck priced under $1 million.

Guess where this one is sold:

  1. Maryland
  2. Virginia
  3. D.C.
We’ll let you know tomorrow how many of you got it right.





SPORTS

Want to know what offseason moves could be in store for the upstart Mystics? Or perhaps you’re curious if this season’s Capitals team is a legitimate Stanley Cup contender. Well, you’re in luck! The Sun’s Emma Baccellieri is hosting a Reddit AMA today at 1:30 p.m., so join in so that you can ask her … well, anything!

The Commanders finally have some good news on the injury front: After missing the past two games, quarterback Jayden Daniels is expected to return to the lineup this Sunday against the Giants.

“The goal is for [Daniels] to have a full week of practice and start on Sunday,” head coach Dan Quinn said Monday.

Even better for Washington fans: Daniels will be joined in his return by right guard Sam Cosmi, safety Nick Cross and running back Rachaad White.

entries.title: Morning Sun: What They’re Talking About
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Messaging check-in. Democrats court the young men electorate. And: Parents of young children in Congress say they need help. 





THE LATEST

The Epstein longtail: Last year, when Democrats were first laser-focused on the Jeffrey Epstein story, many party strategists behind the scenes said it was a brief moment in time — it’s not like we’re gonna be running ads about this, they’d say. But the issue has had longer legs than anyone expected. And now Epstein is a big part of the final messaging push in several Democratic races — the Senate Majority PAC is running one in Alaska, the Democratic nominee is on air with one in Kansas and House Democrats’ campaign arm has Epstein’s face in an ad in Pennsylvania’s 1st Congressional District.

The Epstein spots are about painting Republicans as way out of touch with the electorate. “This really has been the central message of ours since day one,” a Democratic strategist familiar with House races told The Washington Sun’s Manuela Silva recently. “You saw that start to gain ground early on in this cycle with Democrats talking about how Republicans have broken their promise to voters.”

Welcome back to Sprint Week, where we’re examining the big questions in the final month before the midterms. Today, let’s talk about closing arguments. Last night in Nebraska, Donald Trump took to the stage to deliver an 81-minute version of his party’s final message. He announced a new plan on diesel fuel, but the overall talking points haven’t changed much since the Republican midterm convention around Labor Day: Trump asked the farm-state crowd to vote like he was on the ballot and again promised to put cold, hard cash in Americans’ pockets if Republicans win. The Sun’s Kadia Goba traveled with the president to Grand Island, Nebraska, and found some skepticism toward his second term even in that audience.

“I don’t care either way if they take illegal people or not,” Yvonne Mora, 66, told Kadia. “They should come here legally, just like we would have to if we went to their country. But one thing’s for sure, I think ICE should definitely not beat them or Taser them and treat them like animals if they are not resisting.” Voters like Mora are why Republican candidates are increasingly trying to change the subject to a Democrats are dangerous and crazy closing message instead.

But the circumstances of this election make that tough. Ad spending tracked by environmental advocacy group Climate Power shows how increasing utility costs have fueled a recent boom in spending around the topic. In the first quarter of the year,

$18.4 million in ads across the country focused on utility bills. The spending hit $138.5 million in the last quarter. Only around 5% of total ad spending is centered on utility costs, the group estimates, but that surge comes by and large from Democratic-affiliated groups. While Republicans are trying to talk about anything other than the economy of the moment, Democrats still have plenty to say.

More: Supreme Court Rejects a Last-Ditch Effort to Block the Paramount-Warner Merger • Trump Says He’ll Pay for Promotional Ads Instead of Taxpayers • NYT: Potential Iranian Drone Attack Led to Exit of U.S. Aircraft from British Air Base





FROM A POTENTIAL FUTURE


Democrats try to understand young men: Is there a world where young, disaffected men trust Democrats to solve their problems? The Sun’s Sam Fortier reports from the second annual Symposium on Young American Men in D.C. (top sponsors: fraternities). Trump made huge gains among young men in 2024, and Sam found a couple of Democrats trying to win them back — Rep. Ro Khanna of California and Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona — among the speakers at the conference. Sam spoke to them, and writes about the various efforts others Democrats have made to connect with the young guys in recent years.

It’s not a simple task, event organizer Ellen Carmichael told Sam. “The right should not take them for granted, and the left should not condescend or cosplay,” she said. “Who’s actually going to meaningfully care about these people as human beings?”





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

Members of Congress with young children believe more of them should be on the Hill but the way the job is structured makes that incredibly difficult, The Sun’s Oriana González reports. “This workplace doesn’t support me having a baby,” said Rep. LaMonica McIver (D-New Jersey), who gave birth last week. Data shows fathers to children under 18 are overrepresented in Congress: 15% of U.S. adults are fathers to young children, compared to 23% of members. Just 7% are mothers to minor children, compared to 18% of the overall U.S. adult population.



More: Trump Approves Firing Squad Execution for Fort Hood Shooter • Supreme Court Rejects Appeal Over School’s Ban on ‘Let’s Go Brandon’ Sweatshirts • MAHA Activists Feel Betrayed by the Farm Bill — And Their GOP Allies

  • Mayors Are Filming Videos, Mamdani-Style, With Varying Degrees of Cringe, by Julie Bosman for The New York Times
  • Pentagon officials’ heated debates foreshadowed problems in Iran, by Dan Lamothe, Rachel Chason and Suzan Haidamous for The Washington Post

entries.content:
Aren’t we all looking for an escape sometimes? A roof deck might be just the answer, especially if you listen to The Drifters: “On the roof, it's peaceful as can be, and there the world below can't bother me.”

Whether you’re sipping morning coffee as the sun rises or a martini as the sun sets, a terrace in the sky can make you feel like you’re a millionaire even if you’re not. (Of course, for the utmost in rooftop glamor, someone may want to snap up the home at 99 Observatory Circle in Northwest D.C., which has an extensive private roof terrace facing west for sunset views. But that one will cost $9.5 million.)

For the rest of us, here are some options for a home with a private or shared roof deck priced under $1 million.



Which one would you choose? Or, have a comparison you’d like to see in an upcoming column? Let us know at metro@washingtonsun.com.



D.C.

Untitled
The listing: City Vista 475 K St. NW, Unit 615

The price: $965,000

The specifics: This 1,433-square-foot three-bedroom, three-bathroom condo in the K at City Vista is the largest unit in the 11-story building, which has a grocery store, gym, salon, spa and restaurants downstairs.

The roof deck: The shared roof deck includes spectacular city views, couches, a grill, tables where you can sneak up to work on a sunny day, plus a pool and a hot tub. Other building amenities include a green space on the third floor, a business center and a party room. Just be prepared to pay $1,005 a month in condo fees.

What makes it special: The unit includes floor-to-ceiling windows, a balcony and has south-facing windows with city views. Located in the Mount Vernon Triangle neighborhood, it’s walkable to three Metro stations plus shops and restaurants.

Agent: Jennifer Tugberk, TTR | Sotheby's International Realty

Maryland

Untitled
The listing: 820 Thompson Crescent Unit 26, Rockville

The price: $839,000

The specifics: This townhouse, built in 2020, is over 2,550 square feet with three bedrooms, including two primary suites. The four-level townhouse has a bathroom on each floor, including three full bathrooms and two half-bathrooms.

The roof deck: The top level has a recreation room that opens to a private roof terrace, which has sunset views and space for relaxing and entertaining.

What makes it special: The townhouse has flexible spaces for a home office and a gym. The living level has 9-foot-high ceilings, wide-plank hardwood floors and large windows. This is the largest townhouse model in Chapman Row, located two blocks from the Twinbrook Metro station and close to the Pike & Rose development for shops, restaurants and entertainment, as well as other shopping options. Monthly homeowner association fees here are $414.

Agent: Danielle Mannix, Compass

 

Virginia

Untitled
The listing: 10449 Breckinridge Lane, Fairfax

The price: $923,000

The specifics: This 2,628-square-foot brick-colonial-style townhouse has three bedrooms and four bathrooms. The townhouse has a two-car garage and two additional parking spaces.

The roof deck: Two sliding glass doors lead from an upper-level loft sitting area with a fireplace to a private roof deck with treetop views. Open both sets of doors, and you have an elevated indoor-outdoor living space.

What makes it special: Besides the roof deck, this home has an enclosed stone patio for outdoor entertaining. The traditional floor plan includes another fireplace in the living room, hardwood floors and high ceilings. The four-level home is in a landscaped community with green spaces and a gazebo, and it’s within walking distance of the City of Fairfax Historic District, shops and restaurants. Monthly homeowner association fees are $135.

entries.title: As Food Insecurity Grows, D.C. Groups Are Helping Residents Keep Benefits
entries.summary: Food pantries have seen an uptick in demand in the last year amid limited access to federal programs.
entries.content:
Tucked behind the laundry room at an apartment complex in Southeast D.C. lies Fresh Market at Washington View. Twice a week, this unique resource offers free essential and specialty food products to D.C. residents who registered for the service. On a recent afternoon, one patron entered rattling off a highly specific list.

“I need steak, lobster, gift cards, my rent paid this month,” he said as the neighbors who staff the pantry hyped him up. “Gas bill! Water bill!” He settled on applesauce, cornbread mix, one bottle of water and grapes.

Local nonprofit Building Bridges Across the River opened the market in 2024 in collaboration with 15 corporate partners and with input from residents of the apartment complex. The market began offering produce and protein in 2025 through the Freshfarm Food Hub, a nonprofit that sources from farmers across Maryland, Virginia and Pennsylvania. Lately, there has been a significant uptick in visits from residents.

Carrie Vaughn, farm director with Building Bridges Across the River, said the market “probably [has] twice as many people coming now per week as we had this time last year.”

A need to connect residents to resources has been growing across the District over the last year as access to Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and Medicaid benefits became sharply limited through the Trump-backed “one big, beautiful bill.”

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

As previously reported by The Washington Sun, the Capitol Area Food Bank’s 2026 Hunger Report found that more than one in three households across the capital region experienced food insecurity in the past year. According to the report’s heat map, the greatest food distribution in D.C. occurred in Ward 8.

More than 9,000 D.C. residents lost their SNAP benefits from July 2025, when changes to the program’s eligibility requirements went into effect, to June 2026, according to the Food Research and Action Center. Many people, including the elderly, now face an increased work requirement to qualify.

“With SNAP, we've got older folks who have never had to pull together documentation to prove that they are eligible for the food assistance, and now they have to,” said Naseema Shafi, health CEO of the Whitman-Walker clinic. “We know from the different food access reports that our elders in the community are some of our most food insecure.”

Vaughn, who said her organization began restructuring its approach to community support after dealing with a surge of need during the government shutdown last year, said “once we saw that changes to SNAP were coming, we didn't want to be as reactive as we were last year.”

For Washington View resident Angela Clemons, a mother of three who is both a patron and an employee of the food pantry, having help maintaining benefits and keeping food on the table is vital for her family. “People are gonna really need the pantry because if you're not working, then you can't get SNAP,” she said. “And it’s hard to find a job.”
food_pantry_02.jpg (5512x3675, AR: 1.50)To counter the effects of the economic and policy changes, Building Bridges partnered with seven organizations to create another collaborative. The network’s workforce and wellness initiative helps eligible residents keep their benefits by providing workforce training, assisting with paperwork, identifying exemptions and maintaining access to resources like Fresh Market.

“The reason workforce and wellness came together was because we're helper organizations,” Shafi said. “We think we can do something really impactful when we're working across our sectors. People can find someone who can help them navigate these really difficult things.”

The organizations are also working to identify and help especially vulnerable residents, including immigrants, whose ability to obtain legal residency can depend on whether they have received social safety benefits. The public charge policy “has made people feel like they can't access benefits that they're entitled to,” Shafi said. “They're afraid that it'll get counted negatively on their immigration journey.”

Shafi said the network is also looking to identify less obvious vulnerable demographics, including childless, single men. “We have a lot of men in our community who don't access health care until they're really sick, and we have a lot of men in our community who are facing so many other barriers,” Shafi said. “This is a lot more burden on them, too.”

As policies and requirements evolve, the organizations continue to assist residents in qualifying for benefits and filling gaps in coverage. Building Bridges CEO Scott Kratz said the initiative is now ramping up efforts to provide resources as the deadline to meet new work requirements or qualify for Medicaid exemptions approaches.

“These community health care workers can help to make sure that they get exempted,” he said of work requirements for assistance programs. “If they’re exempt [from SNAP], that also could exempt them from Medicaid cuts starting in January.”

entries.title: The Worst Workplace to Become a Parent? Congress.
entries.summary: The lack of support for young parents is something Rep. LaMonica McIver said “keeps me up at night.”
entries.content:
Rep. LaMonica McIver of New Jersey gave birth to a baby girl last week, becoming just the 15th voting member of Congress in history to give birth while serving in office.

But months before, the freshman lawmaker was already worried about how she would be able to raise a child while also serving in an institution that has no flexibility for working parents.

“That really keeps me up at night,” McIver said.

McIver told The Washington Sun in mid-August, when she was eight months pregnant, that “this is my first job ever where I don’t get any support as an expecting mom when I deliver my kid.”

“I've been spending most of my time trying to plan what that looks like, so I'm there healing properly, spending time with my incoming child, but also how do I continue to show up for my constituents and and be present in voting, because I know that this workplace doesn't support me having a baby,” McIver said.

Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Washington), the mother of a young son, told the House Rules Committee recently that “the representation of the body is improved when we have a more representative body. I believe there are fewer than 10 members of Congress who have a child in day care. Is it any shock then that day care has not become a priority of this body?”

Mothers of young children are underrepresented in Congress: While 18% of all U.S. adults are mothers of children under 18, only 7% of members of Congress — 39 lawmakers — are mothers of young children, according to data from the Vote Mama Foundation.

https://x.com/RepLaMonica/status/2105700936857333913?s=20

AOC and Other Lawmakers Publicly Talk About Decisions to Plan for a Family

In recent years, more female House lawmakers have opened up about their decisions to start a family. Rep. Sara Jacobs (D-California) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York) have talked about their egg-freezing journeys. Ocasio-Cortez documented her procedures on social media, sharing a lot of personal details about the process.

Rep. Kat Cammack (R-Florida), who gave birth to her son last year, revealed that she had an ectopic pregnancy. Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-California) disclosed that she’d had a miscarriage.

The Washington Sun spoke with four lawmakers and candidates from both parties who opened up about their reproductive health decisions, and juggling becoming a parent and serving as a member of Congress. They all focused on the same message: More parents of young children should run and serve in office.

“There are a lot of issues and, respectfully to my colleagues who are on the back nine here, some of them, they certainly have grandchildren, and in some cases, great-grandchildren, but I don’t think they can fully appreciate some of the challenges of parenthood today,” Rep. Mike Lawler (R-New York) told The Sun in an interview. “Having young parents in Congress matters. It’s important for the debate, for the discussion, for public policy.”

Lawler, who is the father of two young daughters, has talked about his and his wife’s struggle to conceive. He told The Sun that he and his wife had a second miscarriage this year. His experience led him to co-sponsor legislation aimed at expanding access to assisted reproductive technologies, such as in vitro fertilization.

Renewed Push for Proxy Voting for New Parents

Lawmakers still get paid if they’re absent, but they cannot vote on legislation if they’re not present in the House chamber. In 2025, a bipartisan effort to allow new parents to vote remotely for 12 weeks after birth failed after Speaker Mike Johnson called proxy voting “unconstitutional.” Lawmakers renewed the push last month, when they urged the House Rules Committee to consider adding proxy voting for new parents in the rules for the upcoming Congress next year.

“For many of us on the West Coast, we are on round-trip flights for 12 hours total, often two, three, sometimes four times a month. You literally are not allowed to fly at some point in your pregnancy; imagine doing that with a newborn who needs their parent around,” Jacobs said at the hearing.

“Proxy voting is so important, for me it’s literally going to decide if or when I can start my own family, and I know that’s true for many others,” Jacobs added.

Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Michigan) didn’t give birth while serving in office but said she has school-aged children, “and the demands on our time for being in this body and also being at home should not be understated. And I’ve heard many say, ‘Well, then maybe you should choose a different profession.’ That would be an incredible disservice to the American people. They are underserved when they don’t have voices like ours in Congress to speak on them.”

Lawler, who represents one of the most competitive districts in the country, said that his second daughter was born eight days before the 2024 election. He joined Reps. Brittany Pettersen (D-Colorado), Anna Paulina Luna (R-Florida) and Jacobs in co-leading the failed resolution to allow proxy voting for new parents.

“Not only did I obviously have to campaign in that final week, but then I had to show up and be back on the House floor the following week. So I never had a week or two weeks or even a day off in that immediate aftermath,” Lawler recounted. “For my female colleagues, that’s obviously even worse.”

Pettersen made history in April last year when she held her newborn son, Sam, during an official floor speech. He was just 9 weeks old.

U.S. Congress (4500x3000, AR: 1.50)
The congresswoman first brought Sam to the House floor when he was 4 weeks old, traveling to the Capitol to vote against President Donald Trump’s One Big, Beautiful Bill. Pettersen told the House Rules Committee in September that by the time Sam was 6 months old, he had taken 24 flights. While infants can physically withstand flying after the first week of life, medical experts recommend waiting until a baby is 2 to 3 months old, when they’ve developed stronger immunity.

“It’s the system that makes it so difficult to get there to begin with and continue to serve as a mom that we need to change,” Pettersen told The Sun.

Pettersen said that it was important for her to share her experience to inspire “people to believe that they can also continue to step into these roles even when they have children.” But she admitted her public push has subjected her to a lot of backlash.

“The amount of people that have said that I should be home, I should be taking care of my kids, I shouldn’t be in Congress, is shocking how pervasive that is,” Pettersen said. She added that the criticism has come from Republicans, online comments and even current members of Congress.

McIver, who faces up to 17 years in prison after being indicted over an incident outside an immigration detention center, recalled that after she announced she was pregnant in May, she started seeing people make “memes” of her “with a baby bump in a prison suit behind bars.” Others said “cruel and racist things as well, like, ‘Another Black ghetto baby coming into this world.’ I mean, you name it, you can take a walk if you like through my social media comments. They’re honestly disgusting,” she said.

Candidates See Running as a Parent as a Positive

While Pettersen and McIver said they’ve met moms who’ve told them that they don’t believe they could run for office, some candidates are touting their roles as parents on the campaign trail.

Rebecca Bennett, the Democrat running against Rep. Tom Kean Jr. (R-New Jersey), has made her role as a mom to two young daughters, who are 4 and 7 years old, a major pitch in her campaign. She includes capping child care costs, providing 12 weeks of paid family leave and providing funding for universal pre-K among her policy priorities.

“There are currently only five moms with kids under 6 in Congress right now,” Bennett said. “This is why we need more people in office that really understand the challenges that families are facing. When people are talking about the affordability crisis, those are not talking points for me. This is my life.”

Her campaign organizes meet and greets at playgrounds on Friday afternoons and Saturday mornings, “because if you have young kids, it’s very difficult to come out to a political event at seven o’clock in the evening.”

As a former Navy helicopter pilot, she thinks a lot about the high rates of infertility among veterans. She told The Sun that after having her first daughter, she had a miscarriage.

“When I started sharing with my friends that I had one, they all told me they had one too, but it’s one of those things people don’t talk about because there’s such stigma. So I think the more we can to help break that down, I think the better we’ll be longer term,” Bennett said.

“The more we can share our stories and be able to have people see themselves in our elected officials, I think, is important,” she added.

Lawmakers are helping their colleagues push to change the culture on Capitol Hill to allow for better work-life balance.

Last week, McIver’s staff sent other member offices talking points about the congresswoman’s new baby, according to an email viewed by The Sun. The email contained tweet drafts, graphics templates and video scripts for lawmakers to show support for McIver.

“LaMonica McIver isn’t the first woman to give birth while serving in Congress, but she’s a part of a really small group … Congress isn’t set up for new parents,” one of the video scripts reads. “Let’s stand together and demand inclusive work environments for mothers nationwide and right here in D.C., so we can help the people who count on us.”

entries.title: Washington Tries to Tackle a ‘Crisis Among Young Men’
entries.summary: C-SPAN, panels and polling: Two days of “making space for men” at a conference in Washington.
entries.content:
Look, politicians have tried to meet young men where they are for years and years.

Shock-jockin’, pickup-truckin’, trend-hoppin’ or video-game-streamin’ — they’re willing to do almost anything to reach them, even if it means pretending to know ball (because let’s face it, they do not). So when the political class again looked out and wondered where the young men were and how to get them to vote, the consultants knew just what to do: go to a conference.

The second annual Symposium on Young American Men took place in late September in a bright penthouse near Union Station in Washington. The top sponsors of the event were fraternities. A few panels were broadcast live on C-SPAN. Organizations tabling outside gave away baby-blue buttons (“Gender Equality for Men”), magazines featuring women in lingerie (“the conservative Cosmo”) and sheets stuffed with charts and data tables (“12 Areas of Male Disadvantage”).

Over two days, intellectuals and elected leaders discussed the issues fueling the “crisis among young men” — education, the economy, mental health and lack of community. A pollster laid out new data: Young male voters are back up for grabs! Pay attention to them!

Young men probably won’t play a huge role in the midterm elections, several political operatives said, because they are, as a group, a relatively small and unreliable voting bloc. But they could have outsize influence in a bigger election with smaller margins.

President Donald Trump made massive gains among young men in 2024 — a 15-point swing from 2020 — because they believed he would improve the economy and their job prospects, according to a Tufts University analysis.

But those gains have disappeared, according to a new Cygnal poll released alongside the symposium. More young men now view the GOP unfavorably (49%) than favorably (40%), and among those who say they’re determined to vote, Democrats have a sizable lead (57% to 40%).

Now, Vice President JD Vance is embracing a 22-year-old evangelical with over a million followers on young men’s favorite internet platform (YouTube). And every Democrat potentially vying for the 2028 nomination is trying to do something:

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro has enacted male-friendly policies; Maryland Gov. Wes Moore cozied up to sports teams; and Govs. Gavin Newsom of California and Andy Beshear of Kentucky did podcasts with thought leaders such as the author Richard V. Reeves and NYU professor Scott Galloway on the struggles facing men and boys.

And Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Arizona) and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California) stopped by the symposium to discuss jobs and “making space for men.”

“Back in the day, I was like the only one,” Gallego said of Democrats concerned about young male voters. “Now it seems everyone every week is coming up with a new position, new idea, which is great.”

Republicans lost their 2024 gains among young men because the economy didn’t get better and the Trump administration’s foreign policy approach in Iran and Venezuela has been unpopular, in part because it has raised gas prices, according to lead Cygnal pollster Alex Tarascio.

During focus groups, Tarascio showed older Republicans data on the systemic problems facing younger Americans.

“They'll say, ‘Totally, I see this, this is real,’” he said. Sometimes, their own children had delayed moving out of the house or having kids because it was too expensive. But at some point in every conversation, Tarascio said, they would revert to the avocado-toast ideology: “Well, you know, they just need to save their money a little bit more, and then they can afford a downpayment.”

The older Republican set didn’t “actually believe things are worse now,” he said.

The conversations reminded Tarascio of another finding: Even young men who identify as Republican believe the federal government should do more to help young people.

“For the Republican Party, they're going to have an awakening at some point as these older, small-government ideological people die and the new cohort comes up,” he said.

But just saying the right words to appeal to men isn’t enough, according to Ellen Carmichael, whose firm, The Lafayette Company, organized the event. She argued some Democrats trying to appeal to young men come off as phony — like when a New York Times analysis found they were swearing a lot more.

“The right should not take them for granted, and the left should not condescend or cosplay,” she said. “Who's actually going to meaningfully care about these people as human beings?”

Everyone broadly agreed that young men need help: They are lonely, feel purposeless and often believe they don’t have the power to change it. Gallego extolled the virtues of fraternities — he was in Sigma Chi at Harvard — as a haven for young men, and he co-sponsored a bill to prevent colleges and universities from penalizing or restricting students involved in single-sex social organizations.

“Setting up the environment where these men can meet and talk is important,” he said.

A week after the symposium, young men were back at the center of the news cycle. A former Cornell University student filed a lawsuit alleging she was gang-raped by members of the Chi Phi fraternity in 2024 and that the university failed to protect her. The Lafayette Company, which represents a variety of men’s groups and fraternities, has since signed on to do media relations work for the national Chi Phi organization. Chi Phi said in a statement that it moved quickly to expel those at Cornell “suspected of betraying the values of our brotherhood.”

Khanna was one of the few 2028 contenders to weigh in publicly on the case thus far, posting a video on social media decrying a “crisis of misogyny.” In a statement to The Washington Sun, Gallego called the alleged events at Cornell “horrific.”

“Women should feel safe on campus whether in class, at the dining hall, or at a party — no ‘if’s, ‘and’s’ or ‘buts’ about it,” he said.

Gallego, 46, was at the symposium last fall, when it was just a one-day event, and criticized members of his own party for underappreciating the value of having a father in a child’s life (he grew up without a dad) and said the broad application of the term “toxic masculinity” has “gone too far.” He championed a bill he co-sponsored that would create an Office of Men’s Health.

“It caused some controversy with former newscasters,” Gallego said, referring to online criticism from Katie Couric. “But it’s important.”

The moderator, political journalist Ben Jacobs, prodded Gallego to directly address Couric.

“Sen. Gallego, I know you said that you’re championing men’s health because you want to be a good father,” Couric had said of his legislation. “But I think one of the best ways to show up for your family is to ensure your daughter and wife have access to the same quality of care and information and research as you and your sons.”

“It’s not worth it,” Gallego said a couple times, turning the discussion back to the importance of male mentors and improving the economy for working-class families.

“The real buying power of the working man has declined tremendously over the last 40 years,” he said, comparing it to the downward trend of the average life expectancy of men. “Unless we change how men and women are paid, where they’re actually going to be able to make a living, spend time with their families and not be so stressed out all the time … then this will continue to happen.”

And then there was Khanna, 50, who the way to win young men was actually about the economy.

“No war, no aid to Israel and actually caring about jobs here and communities here,” Khanna said of his pitch to young men. “We [need to] have a good jobs agenda so that young men have good jobs.”

Khanna, one of the most progressive members of his party, sat next to Grover Norquist, 69, a longtime anti-tax conservative activist on a panel. It was the closest thing to a cage match you can get in downtown D.C. — well, besides the actual cage match held on the White House lawn. They sparred over whether the government should intervene to help rural communities abandoned by corporations before turning to whether taxes inhibit job creation.

California is “stealing” money from billionaires through higher property tax rates, Norquist said, which would “begin to hollow out” Silicon Valley.

“One-third of the wealth is in my district — literally of the country,” Khanna fired back, rattling off statistics and name-checking a couple famous AI executives. “The question is: Who is this country going to work for?”

“I used to live in Massachusetts, and that’s the attitude we had about Polaroid, which is now bankrupt,” Norquist said.

As Khanna left the stage, a man with white hair rushed up. He applauded one of Khanna’s old bills, introduced but never passed, to help reindustrialize the nation. The man urged Khanna to keep fighting, to keep pushing his ideas, because he believed those jobs were the future.

The way men were, he said, was the way men could be again.

entries.summary: The collision happened in Petworth around 7 p.m. Monday.
entries.content:
A man is in critical condition after being hit by a Metrobus while crossing a street in Petworth on Monday evening.

A bus traveling the D74 route struck the pedestrian at around 7 p.m. near the intersection of Georgia Avenue NW and New Hampshire Avenue NW, according to the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority.

entries.title: Ed Cooley Defends Georgetown’s ‘Mystique’ Ahead of Pivotal Season
entries.summary: The Hoyas coach completely rebuilt the team’s roster this offseason, knowing it needs to post better results entering his fourth season in charge.
entries.content:
NEW YORK — Ed Cooley still believes the Georgetown brand is strong despite the Hoyas’ fall from the ranks of college basketball’s premier programs over the past 20 years.

Cooley spoke at Big East media days last week, where the program was picked to finish 10th in the 11-team conference, with no players receiving any preseason all-conference honors. The Rhode Island native is 42-57 in three seasons coaching Georgetown, after a 12-year run with Providence that included seven NCAA Tournament appearances.

As Cooley enters a pivotal fourth season, he defended the program’s brand and strength, despite the lack of recent success.

“Absolutely the mystique is not gone,” Cooley said. “Absolutely not. Yeah, have we had some turbulent waters? We haven't had the success that we want — absolutely. But the mystique will never go away. You can't erase history. You can't erase dominance. You can't erase Hall of Famers. We have not done what I wish we would do and there's a lot of variations and reasons why — zero excuses. Year four we need to make a big jump. There's no hiding behind a lack of success. We have to do a better job.”

Georgetown hasn’t been to the NCAA tournament since 2021, when an improbable run to the Big East Tournament title propelled Patrick Ewing into his lone Big Dance appearance as the program’s coach. The Hoyas haven’t been to the second weekend of the tournament since the 2007 Final Four, which was in John Thompson III’s third year.

Cooley took over a Georgetown program that hardly resembled the one from Thompson’s early tenure. The Hoyas won a combined 13 games in Ewing’s last two seasons from 2021 to 2023. Cooley left Providence, which he had turned into a perennial conference contender, to undertake a massive rebuild.

The Hoyas haven’t even been a bubble team under Cooley, and went 16-18 last season. Cooley cited injuries and late-game execution as two reasons the program has struggled to win under him. He has a point. The Hoyas lost KJ Lewis in February due to an ankle injury, depriving them of their leading scorer going into March. A year earlier, center Julius Halaifonua missed the majority of the season due to a foot injury.

To get things on track this season, Cooley’s staff prioritized experience, shooting and “know-how” as they assembled this season’s team.

“Those were the marching orders to try and build this roster,” Cooley said.

The result is eight newcomers and 11 departures, giving Cooley a completely remade roster. The Hoyas added additional ball handlers such as Jaland Lowe (Kentucky) and Elmarko Jackson (Kansas), two players who were highly touted out of high school but have had mixed success in college. Cooley predicted that Jackson would be one of the conference’s best on-ball defenders.

Lowe is coming off of shoulder surgery for an injury that limited him to nine games at Kentucky last season. When healthy, he could be one of the Hoyas’ best scorers and playmakers.

“The last college player I had that had a shoulder injury was the No. 5 pick in the NBA draft,” Cooley said of Lowe. “If his shoulder is anything like Kris Dunn’s, then I’m going to love coaching this kid.”

Injuries and availability remain concerns as the Hoyas enter the season. Cooley said Lowe, Kayvaun Mulready and Caleb Williams, the latter a Sidwell Friends graduate, were not healthy over the summer. Two international players did not arrive until August.

The Hoyas are also awaiting word on St. John’s transfer Vince Iwuchukwu, who was granted a temporary restraining order by a New York court to play this season, but could have his eligibility overturned. Cooley said the program doesn’t know when that situation could be resolved. Iwuchukwu went into cardiac arrest while at Southern California and has missed close to a full season over his career due to health issues, which is why Cooley said he has a strong case to be granted another year of eligibility.

Mulready signed with Providence out of high school, before electing to follow Cooley down I-95 to Georgetown. The junior guard said Cooley told him it would be a multiyear rebuild and his coach has done a good job of addressing last year’s issues with the current team.

“Sometimes we get yelled at for passing up open shots,” Mulready said in an interview with The Washington Sun. “But it’s a great problem to have. There’s a lot more options offensively around the perimeter.”

Whether Cooley is coaching for his job this season is unclear. Georgetown President Eduardo M. Peñalver started the role in July after a tenure at Seattle University, a school not known for its basketball success. But Cooley knows that no matter what, the program needs to take a step forward after years of national irrelevance.

“‘Can we finish the mission?’ is what our goal is with this group,” Cooley said.

entries.title: Democrats Cut Their Ad Spending in North Carolina After Republican Retreat
entries.summary: WinSenate, an affiliated super PAC of the Senate Majority PAC, has removed about $1.1 million in reservations, according to the tracking firm AdImpact.
entries.content:
A major Democratic Senate super PAC is trimming its advertising in North Carolina, days after Republicans made a much larger retreat from the state’s Senate race.

WinSenate, an affiliated super PAC of the Senate Majority PAC, has removed about $1.1 million in reservations while keeping $18.8 million booked through Election Day, according to the tracking firm AdImpact.

The decision comes as recent public polling has consistently shown former Gov. Roy Cooper ahead of Republican Michael Whatley.

Democrats’ pullback from North Carolina follows a much larger Republican retreat, with the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC supporting Republican Senate candidates, scrapping about $18 million in planned North Carolina advertising on Friday.

The sum represents a significant pullback for the group, which had already spent about $32 million there.

Instead, the group is shifting its money elsewhere. Axios reported Tuesday that the Senate Leadership Fund is putting $5 million into South Carolina, and spending nearly $8.2 million in Kansas to support Republican Sen. Roger Marshall against Democrat Adam Hamilton.

Other Republican groups have also canceled North Carolina reservations, leaving Whatley with less outside support in the final stretch of the race.

WinSenate has been one of the biggest Democratic outside spenders in Senate races this year. The group has run ads in North Carolina as well as Ohio, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire and other states.

North Carolina remains one of the Democratic Party’s biggest investments. Senate Majority PAC initially announced $31.4 million in North Carolina television reservations in May and added another $11 million in July, bringing its announced television investment in the state above $42 million. It has also spent on digital advertising.

Cooper and Whatley are competing to replace Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who is retiring, in the Nov. 3 election.

entries.title: U.K. Police Arrest a Seventh Man in Connection With Terror Plot at U.S. Air Base
entries.summary: Six others have been released on bail under investigation.
entries.content:
By Jill Lawless

LONDON (AP) — British police on Tuesday arrested a 22-year-old man in London on suspicion of a terror offense over a security incident at a U.S.-run military air base in England that authorities have linked to Iran.

The arrest is the seventh in connection with a suspected plot against RAF Fairford, located 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran during this year's war.

Counter Terrorism Policing said the man, a British national, was detained in the Westminster area of central London on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts.

Six other men have been released on bail under investigation.

Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counterterrorism policing said detectives “continue to pursue multiple lines of enquiry” and “remain committed to investigating all possible angles.”

Scores of residents were evacuated from their homes near the base early on Sept. 27 as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swooped on the rural area. Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant — gasoline — in three vans linked to the five suspects, but no explosives.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the U.K. sees “strong indications” that Iran played a part in the incident, without saying why or what the nature of the suspected plot was.

Iran has denied involvement, but it has previously said it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.

The U.S. moved its B-52 and B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford on Sunday, though it's unclear whether the move is connected to the arrests. President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that he didn’t want to tempt “the enemy” by having the bombers there.

“We had a threat, and if we’re going to be threatened, we would just move them, and that sort of alleviates that,” he said in Washington. He said that the people who made the threat “would be linked to Iran,” but he didn’t offer details.

entries.title: Anduril Plans a $3.7 Billion Baltimore Shipyard for Virginia-Class Submarines
entries.summary: Donald Trump will announce the project at the former Bethlehem Steel site.
entries.content:
Anduril Industries plans to invest $3.7 billion to build a massive new shipyard in Baltimore to produce sections of Virginia-class attack submarines. The project marks a return to large-scale shipbuilding at a site where Bethlehem Steel once built ships for the U.S. military.

The 2-million-square-foot facility at Sparrows Point is expected to create 14,000 jobs, including more than 3,100 permanent jobs and thousands more indirect and construction jobs, company executives, Trump administration officials and Maryland Gov. Wes Moore told reporters. Anduril expects the shipyard, dubbed Arsenal-2, to begin hiring in 2029 and launch operations in 2030.

President Donald Trump is expected to formally announce the project Tuesday alongside Anduril executives and senior Navy and Pentagon officials. The Navy has awarded Anduril a production contract of up to $2.9 billion for submarine components and not the facility itself, with federal funding expected to come through future budgets.

“This is a massive new project that's going to deliver the largest private investment and create the most jobs in Maryland in well over a decade, and so that makes it one of the largest economic projects in our state's history,” Moore said. “One interesting fact is that this project is going to bring more jobs back to Sparrows Point than were retained by Bethlehem Steel in the last half century.”

The Bethlehem Steel mill at Sparrows Point in Baltimore County permanently closed in 2012, and the site has since been redeveloped into the 3,300-acre Tradepoint Atlantic, a logistics and industrial hub. Anduril said it has a long-term lease with Tradepoint.

The new investment comes as the Navy struggles to increase production of Virginia-class submarines, which are nuclear-powered boats designed to hunt enemy submarines and ships, conduct surveillance and strike targets on land.Administration officials said the Anduril facility would add about a 15 percent increase in production capacity. The torpedo tubes Anduril plans to procure are a bottleneck for submarines already under production.

Maryland and Baltimore County have committed to providing incentives worth up to 13% of Anduril’s anticipated private investment through existing economic development programs and new appropriations that would require approval by the Maryland General Assembly and the Baltimore County Council, Moore said. The state also plans to invest in a workforce training center to support the facility.

Anduril’s entry represents a large bet by the fast-growing defense-tech company that has little track record in the heavy industrial work required to build nuclear-powered subs.

Though the Navy typically purchases two Virginia-class submarines each year, the industry has recently been completing only about 1.1 to 1.2 per year. The Anduril shipyard is part of a broader push to catch up to that demand and potentially expand it.

The Pentagon and Congress have poured billions of dollars into expanding the submarine industrial base, which includes the shipyards, suppliers and workers needed to build and maintain the fleet. Part of that involves shifting some submarine construction to manufacturers outside of Electric Boat and Newport News, the only two U.S. shipyards that build nuclear-powered ships.

Anduril is best known for autonomous weapons and drones, but the 9-year-old firm is building a 5-million-square-foot complex in Columbus, Ohio, designed to mass-produce missiles, drones and other weapons.

The firm has already begun prototyping torpedo tubes at a facility it is opening in California and plans to move that work to Baltimore as Arsenal-2 comes online. If it can meet the Navy’s certification and safety requirements, it would eventually expand into larger modules and eventually entire bow and stern sections, Anduril President and Chief Strategy Officer Chris Brose said.

Those sections, known in the industry as “super modules,” would be transported by water to General Dynamics Electric Boat in Connecticut and HII’s Newport News Shipbuilding in Virginia, where they would be incorporated into submarines. Those two companies would continue performing final assembly, testing and delivery to the Navy.

Brose acknowledged that the Baltimore project represents a new direction and said the company was initially skeptical when the Navy approached it about joining the Virginia-class program.But he said Anduril executives concluded the company could bring modern manufacturing techniques, software and factory design to an industry facing production bottlenecks and shipyards with aging infrastructure.

“The more we studied this, the deeper we've got into it, the more we realized that as a company we really do have something to offer here, and you know, shame on us if we didn't help,” he said.

Anduril would approach submarine manufacturing in its own way, Brose said, similar to its Arsenal-1 complex. Rather than requiring the highly skilled laborers the industry struggles to find, it would break down portions of the manufacturing process into smaller, simpler jobs that less experienced workers can perform.

“We're going to approach how you build submarines differently,” Brose said. “We're not getting involved in this to build submarines the exact same way that they have been built for decades.”

Correction: A previous version of this article incorrectly described Maryland Gov. Wes Moore’s role in Tuesday’s announcement. He is scheduled to attend a separate announcement in the Tradepoint area later in the day.

entries.title: Trump Does Not Plan to Reimburse the Government for Taxpayer-Funded Ads
entries.summary: The president pledged to pay for the ads himself, but he will not help the government recoup the federal dollars already used for the spots.
entries.content:
The White House confirmed that President Donald Trump does not plan to reimburse the federal government for the taxpayer money already spent on what he’s called “Patriotic Ads,” despite the fact that he pledged on Truth Social to “pay for them myself.”

“The President’s Truth was not referring to reimbursement,” a White House spokesperson told The Washington Sun Tuesday.

The White House has characterized the ads as “Presidential Public service announcements” and said that they “are nothing new,” citing ad campaigns run by former Presidents George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden.

“Administrations of both parties have used public service announcements to explain policy and make the case for the nation’s direction,” the spokesperson said.

In a post Monday on Truth Social, Trump criticized the “Radical Left” for being upset about the campaign-style ads, which heavily feature the president. Trump then committed to paying for the ads himself with the money he has raised through his super PAC, MAGA Inc.

It is technically illegal for a U.S. president to direct the spending decisions of a super PAC under federal campaign-finance law. Trump has frequently called MAGA Inc. — the $400 million super PAC run by his political allies — “my money that I control.”

In another statement sent to The Sun on Monday night, a White House official confirmed that Trump will only pay for the ads “moving forward.”

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have criticized Trump’s ads after reports that the administration used $20 million in Homeland Security funds to pay for the spots.

CNN reported last week that the Trump administration created at least 13 ads, but as of Tuesday, only four have aired.

The first of the four ads, which featured Trump speaking about communism over the song “Love Me,” started airing on Sept. 23. The administration’s latest ad, released Wednesday, centered footage of missile strikes and fighter jets, in an effort to bolster support for the largely unpopular Iran war. All of the broadcast spots say they were “paid for by the U.S. government.”

entries.title: Maine Republican Paul LePage Violates Federal Financial Disclosure Law
entries.summary: The former governor is months late revealing his personal finances. His campaign says Congress will receive the disclosure Tuesday.
entries.content:
Paul LePage, a Republican running to represent Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, is violating the Ethics in Government Act by failing to properly disclose details about his personal finances, a Washington Sun review of federal ethics documents indicates.

LePage, a former Maine governor who is facing Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap, is the latest in a string of high-profile politicians to break federal ethics rules designed to curb conflicts of interest and enhance public transparency.

Lauren LePage, a LePage campaign senior adviser and the candidate’s daughter, confirmed to The Sun on Monday that LePage had not yet filed his required annual financial disclosure, which was due to Congress on May 15. Lauren LePage called the delay “completely unintentional,” a “simple oversight” and a matter the campaign “took immediate steps to correct.”

The LePage campaign provided a FedEx receipt indicating the disclosure should’ve arrived at the Legislative Resource Center, a division of the Office of the U.S. House Clerk, by 10:30 a.m. Tuesday.

Brent Littlefield, a campaign general consultant, separately told The Sun that LePage’s financial disclosure “slipped through the cracks.”

Tom Rust, chief counsel for the House Ethics Committee, declined to comment Monday when The Sun inquired about whether LePage had filed a financial disclosure report.

LePage last disclosed his personal finances in May 2025. At the time, he disclosed a bank account worth between $50,000 and 100,000 and an investment account worth between $100,000 and 250,000. LePage and his wife also reported about $122,000 of income during the previous year, most of which came from Social Security. Also disclosed: a liability of up to $15,000 on a rental property.

LePage, who served as Maine’s governor from 2011 to 2019, could have requested an extension on filing his 2026 financial disclosure but did not, according to congressional records.

Littlefield and Lauren LaPage say Paul LePage’s 2026 disclosure is “consistent” with his 2025 filing, but declined The Sun’s request to review a copy of the 2026 financial disclosure prior to its publication by the Clerk of the House. Paper filing submitted by candidates usually takes the House and Senate more time to publish than electronically submitted disclosures.

In a congressional debate in Maine on Thursday, both LePage and Dunlap, his opponent, said members of Congress shouldn’t be able to trade individual stocks.

This shared sentiment, coupled with LePage’s late disclosure, coincides with the U.S. Senate killing the latest effort to institute a ban on individual stock trading.

President Donald Trump has endorsed LePage, calling him a “winner” who will “not let you down,” and the Cook Political Report has rated the Maine 2nd District race as a “likely Republican” contest.

This isn’t the first time a Trump-endorsed congressional candidate violated federal financial disclosure laws this year: David Flippo, the Republican nominee to represent Nevada’s 2nd Congressional District, failed to disclose his personal finances while self-funding his campaign, The Sun reported in August.

And since the summer of 2025, violators of federal financial disclosure laws in the House include Reps. Gil Cisneros (D-California), Michael Rulli (R-Ohio), Shri Thanedar (D-Michigan), Tracey Mann (R-Kansas), Julie Johnson (D-Texas), Linda Sánchez (D-California), Julia Letlow (R-Louisiana), Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), Lisa McClain (R-Michigan), Pat Ryan (D-New York), Sheri Biggs (R-South Carolina), Derek Tran (D-California), Donald Norcross (D-New Jersey), Tim Walberg (R-Michigan), Rich McCormick (R-Georgia), Ritchie Torres (D-New York), Troy Nehls (R-Texas), Dan Meuser (R-Pennsylvania), Jonathan Jackson (D-Illinois), George Whitesides (D-California), Val Hoyle (D-Oregon), Austin Scott (R-Georgia), Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-Florida), Pramila Jayapal (D-Washington), Kelly Morrison (D-Minnesota), Christian Menefee (D-Texas), Daniel Webster (R-Florida), Ed Case (D-Hawaii), Laurel Lee (R-Florida) and Scott Franklin (R-Florida).

Rep. Kevin Hern (R-Oklahoma) was also late, although his office denies it, and Dan Crenshaw (R-Texas) violated the STOCK Act earlier this year by failing to properly disclose personal stock trades.
