entries.title: Whistleblower Alleges the FBI Carried Out an Illegal Probe of ICE Protesters
entries.summary: The disclosure also alleges that personnel were diverted from investigations involving violent crime, drug trafficking and transnational criminal organizations.
entries.content:
A former FBI supervisor has come forward to allege that President Donald Trump pushed the bureau to investigate anti-ICE protesters in Los Angeles after agents found no evidence they had committed a crime.

Jill Fields, a former supervisory intelligence analyst in the FBI’s Los Angeles field office, made the allegation in a new whistleblower disclosure sent to Sens. Alex Padilla and John Cornyn, the top Democrat and Republican on the Senate Judiciary Committee’s immigration panel.

She is asking Congress and the Justice Department’s inspector general to investigate.

The disclosure describes two instances in early 2025 when Fields says senior administration officials pushed the FBI to investigate protesters, despite concerns inside the bureau that their conduct was protected by the First Amendment, according to Padilla’s letter summarizing the disclosure.

In one incident, Trump had watched a TikTok video of protesters using bullhorns to warn residents about immigration officers in Alhambra, California, and tell them about their legal rights. FBI personnel who reviewed the incident had not found evidence of a crime.

The White House then instructed FBI Director Kash Patel to have the Los Angeles field office investigate the protesters.

Patel later told senior bureau officials that Trump “was angry about the incident, and he wanted those protesters investigated and arrested,” according to CNN, which reviewed the disclosure.

Fields later said she was told by another person, whose name is redacted in the disclosure, that the inquiry would proceed because “the President wants this investigation,” according to NBC News.

The disclosure also alleges a separate push from Emil Bove, the acting deputy attorney general at the time, to investigate anti-ICE and Customs and Border Protection protesters demonstrating at federal buildings in Los Angeles — without identifying a specific crime or national security threat. Bove is now a judge on the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.

Fields and other FBI employees raised concerns that the investigations violated bureau policy and constitutional protections. The disclosure also alleges that personnel were diverted from investigations involving violent crime, drug trafficking and transnational criminal organizations.

Fields had publicly described part of the episode before. In January, she told The New York Times that her team reviewed protesters’ conduct, concluded they had done nothing wrong and were nevertheless told an investigation had to proceed.

Fields also alleges she lost responsibility for three programs after raising objections and believes the action was retaliation for her internal disclosures. She later resigned from the FBI.

In Padilla’s letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche and Patel, he sought details about the investigations and gave them until Oct. 12 to respond. He asked how many demonstrations, social media accounts and people the FBI monitored, whether anyone was arrested or charged, and whether the White House gave instructions concerning the inquiries.

Without control of Congress, Padilla and other Democrats are not able to compel the government to disclose such information — but the focus on potentially unconstitutional investigations of protesters is a likely sign of where the party will focus its efforts should it regain power after November’s midterms.

A Justice Department spokesperson told CNN that the department would continue to “vigorously uphold the First Amendment rights of all Americans and restore the rule of law.”

entries.title: Trump’s Meme Coin Firm Wants You to Buy. Insiders Are Preparing to Sell.
entries.summary: Trump personally made more than $600 million from his meme coin last year.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump's meme coin saw a brief price spike as the crypto firm behind it promoted a major perk for investors: a "gala dinner" attended by the president himself.

But as the company encouraged the public to purchase $TRUMP, the insiders who control the biggest share of the meme coin have prepared to offload substantial portions of their holdings, according to The Washington Sun’s review of public crypto transactions.

Since Sept. 1, the single biggest owner of the cryptocurrency has transferred roughly $70 million worth of $TRUMP to an account that would enable sale of its coins. Experts say such a move would be a necessary first step for whoever controls the creators' shares to dump the meme coin.

The previously unreported transactions have intensified criticisms that those behind the meme coin are aiming to take advantage of Trump’s presidency, as ethics experts remain alarmed by what they see as a president trying to sell a private crypto product.

Trump personally made $1.4 billion on his crypto investments last year, more than $600 million of which came from his meme coin, according to his White House financial disclosures. Zach Everson, the research director at the watchdog group Public Citizen, has calculated that retail investors simultaneously lost $4.7 billion on Trump’s crypto ventures overall.

The recent transfers appear timed to take advantage of the announcement of the gala, which created a rare price bump for a crypto whose value collapsed almost entirely not long after it first debuted.

In a spike of activity, the largest account holder transferred $27 million worth of tokens on Sept. 1, $26 million on Sept. 6, and $18 million on Sept. 20. That enabled their sale just as the crypto company announced plans to hold a gala, attended by Trump and “3 Legends" who have not yet been named, at the Trump National Golf Club in Virginia. The winners will be chosen based on a formula that considers who buys the most $TRUMP in the next two months.

The beginning of the contest triggered a brief spike in the meme coin's price, from around $2.05 to $2.23, and higher than the $1.50 value $TRUMP was trading at for much of the summer. Even that seemingly small a swing in the price could have translated into millions of dollars in profit on the 31 million tokens released since September. The bump has been short-lived, with the price settling back at $2.04 on Tuesday.

The precise identity of the largest account holder is unclear. However, that account holds the vast token pool set aside for the coin's creators, according to Everson. It’s possible that the rights to some or all of those tokens have since been sold or transferred to another entity.

“Regular buyers are urged to hold for a shot at dinner with the president, while tokens reserved for the coin's creators head for the exits,” Everson said. “Tactics like this help explain how investors in Trump's crypto ventures are billions underwater while he’s richer than ever.”

A White House official pushed back on the criticism. The upcoming gala will feature the president and bills itself as “the most exclusive dinner in the world,” but the event invitation also says: “No attendees will be granted a private meet & greet with the President.”

“It is difficult to credibly characterize this as ‘buying access’ to the President when the event organizers have expressly said that no attendee will receive a private meet-and-greet with him,” the official said in a statement. “Even the reporting on prior events found that attendees described themselves primarily as crypto hobbyists and fans. This is a private event — not a government function — and there is no promise of official government action in exchange for attending.”

Bill Zanker, a longtime Trump associate who reportedly launched the Trump meme coin, declined to comment.

Based on how much the president earned from his meme coin, sales so far this year could add another $192 million in profit on top of the $635 million he made last year, according to Corey Frayer, who served as senior adviser to former SEC chair Gary Gensler, who is now the director of investor protection for the Consumer Federation of America.

The company behind the meme coin does not publicly disclose the precise payment arrangement for the president.

“What it looks like is they announce the competition for the dinner, and it drives the meme coin market up so they can sell more fake tokens at even higher prices,” Frayer said. “I don’t know how else you can interpret the transactions.”

Kevin Mercuri, CEO of the public relations agency Propheta Communications, was a spokesperson for Zanker but stopped representing the Trump associate in early 2024. He said he thought Trump’s gala events could have had “positive effects” for the MAGA base when a similar dinner was held last year, but “today the event seems tone-deaf” when “the nation is embroiled in a dead-end war and facing a widespread affordability crisis.”

Nick Pinto, a 26-year-old crypto investor who has lost $400,000 on the Trump meme coin, said he “was shocked” by a copy of the large meme coin transfers sent to him by The Washington Sun. He did not know the owner’s identity but suspected it was Zanker.

In a text, he said: “The grift continues until morale improves."

entries.title: Sen. Chris Murphy Was Denied Entry to a U.S. Military Base in Qatar
entries.summary: The senator is currently on a congressional delegation trip to the Middle East.
entries.content:
Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy was barred from entering a U.S. military base in Qatar, the Connecticut lawmaker told reporters on Tuesday.

The senator is currently on a congressional delegation to the Middle East, where he’s met with key officials to discuss the ongoing Iran war.

During his visit, Murphy traveled to Riyadh, where he met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, and to Qatar, where he met Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani.

“I want to see firsthand the impact of the Iran War, the damage it’s caused to our facilities in the region and how it’s harmed our relationships with partners in the region,” Murphy said in anews release.

As part of his trip, Murphy hoped to visit Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, the largest U.S. Air Force installation in the Middle East.

Reuters first reported that the senator was denied access to the base. The Pentagon also refused to set up a briefing for him on the war.

“This trip confirmed for me that there is an active, unprecedented, unconstitutional effort underway to hide the costs of this war and the implications of this war from Congress and the American people," Murphy told reporters in Riyadh, according to the wire service.

“I've never encountered anything like this in my time in the Senate, and it's part of a deliberate campaign of obfuscation that my Republican colleagues in Congress should demand an end to," he added.

In an emailed statement, a senior Defense Department official told The Washington Sun that Murphy’s office was informed before his trip that he would not receive access to Al Udeid Air Base, citing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s March directive on travel restrictions in the area.

The Defense Department’s legislative affairs office communicated the decision to Murphy’s team, the official said.

“The Department applies the Secretary’s guidance evenly,” the official added.

The base has been repeatedly attacked in the midst of the ongoing conflict.

In March, a missile struck the base but did not cause any casualties, according to Qatar’sMinistry of Defense. In June 2025, U.S. Central Command announced that U.S. forces and their Qatari partners defended against an Iranian ballistic missile attack at the base.

entries.title: Newsom Flags Cybersecurity Concerns After Trump Said Iran Could ‘Take Out’ California Cities
entries.summary: White House communications director Steven Cheung maintains the president’s statements have been widely misinterpreted in the media.
entries.content:
California officials are ramping up security and threat monitoring measures after President Donald Trump suggested that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego while stumping in Nebraska on Monday.

While speaking about the importance of the midterm elections during his rally in Grand Island, the president said that a potential victory in November “verifies all the things we did,” including his war in Iran.

“It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe,” Trump said. “They can take out a city, let ’em take out Los Angeles, let ’em take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay.”

Gov. Gavin Newsom directed state intelligence officials Tuesday to shift focus toward real-time geopolitical intelligence. The California Democrat called Trump’s remarks “dangerous — if not treasonous” and said he is directing the state’s threat assessment center to “monitor the situation in the event that foreign actors interpret the President’s remarks as an invitation to target California.”

Newsom told journalist Jim Acosta that he woke up Tuesday to a call from the head of the California’s Office of Emergency Services alerting him that the department had detected an uptick in concerning cybersecurity activity and threat intelligence.

“Our state operations center had to be lit up because of what the president said,” Newsom said. “And don't think for a second our adversaries aren't listening to that, and trying to manipulate it, and we're seeing it again — real life consequences — the governor of the state of California having to open our state operations center because of the incoming [activity] we're getting as it relates to cybersecurity.”

It is unclear whether Trump’s comments were based on legitimate intelligence, as Iran has never possessed the capability to stage a long-range ballistic missile attack on U.S. soil. But Democrats and some Republicans were quick to decry the statement as an invitation for Iran to attack cities in the country’s biggest blue state.

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said Trump’s move Monday encourages attacks on American lives.

“His statements against our city are dangerous and could potentially compromise our safety,” she said in a statement on X. “In the face of irresponsible threats, as Angelenos, we know how to stand together and protect our city.”

Jim Desmond, a Trump-backed California congressional candidate running to represent a military-heavy district of northern San Diego, said he “vehemently disagreed” with the president.

“No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage,” he said in a post on X.

Trump’s allies were quick to interpret the comments in a different context.

“The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality,” White House communications director Steven Cheung said on X. “He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped. America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money.”

The analysts Newsom asked to turn to geopolitical intelligence will specifically scan for state-sponsored propaganda, foreign intelligence chatter and extremist communications from Iran or its proxies to see if Trump’s statements are being perceived as a strategic vulnerability or an "open invitation" to attack, according to the Office of Emergency Services.

“Cal OES and the State Threat Assessment Center remain vigilant for any potential threats to the state,” department officials said Tuesday. “While there are currently no confirmed threats, we will continue to coordinate with law enforcement partners to support public safety.”

entries.title: FBI Arrests a Suspect Accused of Sending Mike Collins a Death Threat
entries.summary: The suspect was arrested in Buffalo, New York, and is accused of sending a death threat to the Georgia Republican Senate candidate and his son-in-law.
entries.content:
The FBI arrested a man accused of sending a death threat to Rep. Mike Collins, the Georgia Republican running in one of the country’s most competitive U.S. Senate races, and his son-in-law.

The suspect was arrested on Friday and charged with two counts of terroristic threats, according to the sheriff’s office in Butts County, Georgia, which assisted the FBI.

“Threatening to kill a public official or his family is not politics — it is a criminal act, and we will take it seriously and hold those responsible accountable just as we did in this case,” said Butts County Sheriff Gary Long in a statement posted to social media Monday.

The FBI said in an X post Monday that the suspect was arrested in Buffalo, New York.

Butts County Sheriff’s Lt. Matt Munger told The Washington Sun that the suspect had sent a threatening message to Collins on Instagram, and that Collins forwarded the message to the sheriff’s office.

“It’s a rather long message, but it ultimately is just a threat to kill him and his son-in-law,” Munger said.

According to the sheriff's office, the threat was prompted by something the suspect read online about Collins and his son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II.

In the Facebook post, the sheriff’s office wrote that investigators “determined the threat was connected to information in an online story that was not accurate or true.”

Munger said he had not personally seen the story and could not comment on what it said about Collins or his son-in-law.

Collins’ son-in-law has come under scrutiny in the course of the Senate campaign. CNN reported in July that he has a history of posting far-right content online.

The suspect was taken into custody “without incident” outside his home in Buffalo and confessed to sending the message in an interview with law enforcement, Munger said.

The suspect will be charged in Butts County Superior Court, according to Munger, and is expected to have an extradition hearing Wednesday or Thursday.

Collins is running to unseat Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff in the closely watched battleground state. After the CNN report, Ossoff attacked Collins for not addressing his son-in-law’s posts.

The Republican later told The Atlanta Journal-Constitution, “Nobody speaks for me, and I don't speak for anybody else,” and reiterated his support for Israel.

Collins’ campaign did not immediately respond to The Sun’s inquiry.

Collins thanked law enforcement in a post on X on Monday and accused Ossoff of “whipping up” political violence.

“No American should have to worry that their home could be the next Butler, Pennsylvania or Utah Valley University,” Collins said. “I'm grateful to the FBI, the Butts County Sheriff's Department, and all law enforcement partners for acting quickly to protect my family.”

A spokesperson for Ossoff’s campaign said in a statement to The Sun that the senator "condemns all threats of violence."

entries.title: Lawyers for Olympian Cleared in Reflecting Pool Case Demand a Watchdog Probe
entries.summary: The Justice Department inspector general's office declined to comment on whether it would act on the lawyers' request.
entries.content:
By Eric Tucker

WASHINGTON (AP) — Lawyers for a former Olympian whom the Justice Department charged with intentionally damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, only to abruptly drop the case after determining he was not responsible, urged two government watchdogs on Tuesday to examine what they say was a flawed investigation and prosecution.

The attorneys for David Hearn said in a letter to the inspectors general for the departments of Justice and Interior that “incompetence and misconduct" were committed by government officials operating under pressure from President Donald Trump, and that watchdog investigations were needed “to determine what happened inside their agencies that led to the shocking and indefensible treatment” of their client.

The letter was filed days after a District of Columbia judge permanently dismissed the case, ending a brief prosecution derided by defense lawyers and other critics as an abuse of government power pushed by a president who insisted vandalism, not human error, was to blame for damage at the landmark. The request indicates that Hearn's lawyers see an additional need for accountability even after the dismissal of the legal proceedings.

“In light of these findings and the government’s own admissions, a critical purpose of the requested investigations is to collect the facts — through witness interviews and the collection and analysis of electronic media and documents — necessary to hold accountable the individuals and groups who failed Mr. Hearn, the criminal justice system, and the public,” the lawyers wrote.

“These events," they said, "demand accountability and full and unconstrained investigations by your offices.”

The Justice Department inspector general's office declined to comment on whether it would act on the lawyers' request. A phone message seeking comment with the Interior Department's inspector general's office was not immediately returned.

Defense lawyers say prosecutors ignored exculpatory evidence

D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman on Thursday dismissed the case against Hearn with “prejudice,” which would block U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s office from refiling the felony charge against him. He said the decision was warranted by the case's “exceptional circumstances” and agreed with defense attorneys that the government “shot first and asked questions later” by charging Hearn in a "lightning-fast indictment process.”

Pirro moved to dismiss the case in July weeks after it was brought, saying newly produced evidence from the Interior Department showed Hearn was not responsible for damage to the pool’s lining. She attributed the damage instead to a botched installation by a contractor as well as a rush to complete the project in time for this summer’s America 250 celebration in Washington.

But Hearn's lawyers say in their letter that the evidence that established their client's innocence had been in the Justice Department's possession for weeks and was “simply ignored.” They asked the department's inspector general to investigate why prosecutors “rushed to indict” under what they said was political pressure from Trump, who had launched a massive renovation project before the anniversary celebrations and later accused Pirro of having “choked” and “folded like an umbrella" when she dismissed the case.

The attorneys also called on the watchdog to investigate, among other things, whether prosecutors failed to disclose exculpatory information in their possession and prosecutors relied on a grand jury witness who presented an unsupported figure on monetary damages to the pool; whether comments Pirro made at the indictment press conference violated Justice Department policy; and whether Pirro also violated policy by approaching and questioning a defense expert.

“The record reflects an indictment obtained through unusual haste and a prosecution shaped from the outset by political pressure and built on an inadequate investigation," they said, adding, “The sprint to charge Mr. Hearn mirrored the rushed renovation itself, which the President had publicly committed to completing by a fixed deadline.”

Pirro's office did not return an email seeking comment.

Questions are also raised about the Interior Department

Hearn, 67, of Bethesda, Maryland, competed in three Summer Olympics, earning his best finish, ninth, at the 1996 Atlanta Olympic Games, the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee says on its website.

He has said he was on a bike ride on June 19 when he reached in to examine the pool’s newly peeled coating and briefly touched a chunk attached to the side of the pool. But he said he obeyed a park worker’s command to let go of it. He was nonetheless stopped by police officers, arrested and detained for nearly five hours.

He was indicted on one count of property destruction, a charge carrying a maximum 10-year prison sentence.

His lawyers questioned whether prosecutors properly presented the grand jury with adequate evidence to support the charge and the amount of damage alleged by the government.

They say prosecutors failed to “critically examine” allegations of a supposedly key witness whose claims about her interactions with Hearn were contradicted by video evidence, and withheld from the defense team body-worn camera recordings and other evidence.

And they also challenge Pirro herself over her actions, saying she approached a defense expert at the pool on July 17 and asked about his conclusions and the results of his work. No report of that interaction has been produced to defense lawyers, they say.

“A U.S. Attorney who personally interrogates a represented defendant’s testifying expert, in the field, surrounded by her own staff and without notice to counsel, is not gathering evidence — she is testing how the defense intends to prove its case, and doing so in a setting that essentially held the expert captive,” the letter states.

The letter also urges the Interior Department's inspector general to investigate questions including who made the decision “to proceed with an unqualified contractor;" why work on the pool proceeded despite known risks; why the department relied on National Guardsmen to detain Hearn; and why officials made “publicly defamatory” statements even after learning of the dismissal of the case.

Asked for comment, the Interior Department said that “Mr. Hearn admitted to officers that he was tampering with the Reflecting Pool.” His lawyers said in response that Hearn “has never used the word ‘tampering.’ He touched the loose liner in the Reflecting Pool. Big Difference.”

entries.title: Trump Administration to Assign Government Lawyers to Migrant Children's Cases
entries.summary: The move appears to lay the groundwork for one of the biggest changes since guaranteed free legal representation for unaccompanied migrant children was introduced in 2008.
entries.content:
By Gisela Salomon

MIAMI (AP) — The Trump administration is creating a team of attorneys to represent children who traveled alone to the United States in immigration proceedings, which critics say would deprive them of having lawyers who aren't employed by the government and could put them at greater risk of deportation.

The U.S. Health and Human Services Department lawyers will “provide direct legal advice and counsel” to unaccompanied migrant children, according to an announcement in the Federal Register signed by Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The decision, announced last week without fanfare, offered no details beyond that broad mandate.

Health and Human Services said in a statement that its Unaccompanied Alien Children Legal Representation Division will work under its general counsel's direction toward “safely reuniting these children with their families and ensuring they have the legal support they need.”

“This new division will give the Department an additional mechanism to provide these children direct legal support while dedicated public servants work around the clock to safely reunify them with their families,” the department told The Associated Press in a brief statement. It didn't answer additional questions, including whether it would continue to contract with nongovernmental groups for legal representation or when its new legal division is expected to be fully operational.

The move appears to lay the groundwork for one of the biggest changes since guaranteed free legal representation for unaccompanied migrant children was introduced in 2008. It comes after the administration cut ties with the Acacia Center for Justice, a nongovernmental organization that managed 24,000 cases and held a contract to provide representation through a vast network of legal service providers.

The change means migrant children will not have an independent representative to advocate for them who doesn't have a conflict of interest, said Shaina Aber, the Acacia Center's executive director.

“Placing children’s legal representation and services inside of the same agency that holds children in federal immigration custody is an unprecedented step that does not meet basic standards of independence of counsel,” Aber said. It “will only give HHS new opportunities to forsake children’s rights and well-being.”

Wendy Young, president of Kids in Need of Defense, a nonprofit that provides free legal representation and social services to unaccompanied children, called the creation of the new in-house HHS legal team “part of a pattern of attacks that this administration has engaged in, in terms of undermining zealous representation of unaccompanied children in their immigration proceedings.”

The new division will work independently from other government agencies that deal with the minors, including the HHS Office of Refugee Resettlement, which is responsible for the custody and care of the children who arrive in the U.S. without a parent or legal guardian.

There is some precedent for government-paid attorneys defending clients against government prosecutors in civilian and military courts, but as criminal defense lawyers and not in immigration court.

But Young noted that the child's lawyer, the judge, and government attorneys seeking deportation will all be federal employees. Judges are appointed by the Justice Department and prosecutors work at the Department of Homeland Security.

“A government attorney who’s employed by the government most likely would be coached and encouraged to take the position of encouraging the child to agree to voluntary departure and to leave the United States rather than to present a full representation of the facts of their case,” Young said.

Amid the uncertainty, children have been going to their court hearings without legal representation lately, according to advocates.

Americans for Immigrant Justice, another nonprofit that provides free legal representation to unaccompanied immigrant children, said it has been challenging to secure lawyers for the minors since the government suspended funding to legal aid organizations on July 31 through Acacia.

Sui Chung, the group's executive director, said the need for legal representation exceeds the available resources.

“To deny legal counsel to the most vulnerable among us — children who have already fled trauma — is a fundamental breakdown of the fairness our Constitution promises," Chung said. “Children deserve our strongest protection."

The government recently awarded a contract to another organization, Our Rescue, with a potential value of up to $244 million. The transition to Our Rescue, which has been challenged by Acacia, has led to short-term arrangements, including a temporary contract with the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants.

entries.title: Wes Moore Says He Was Blocked From Speaking at Trump’s Baltimore Shipyard Event
entries.summary: The Maryland governor says his administration helped bring a $3.7 billion shipyard project to Baltimore.
entries.content:
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore said he pulled out of President Donald Trump’s event Tuesday to announce plans for a new shipyard in Baltimore after being told he would not be allowed to speak.

The event set for Tuesday afternoon is to announce that Anduril Industries will invest $3.7 billion to open a shipyard at Sparrows Point for Navy submarine parts. Moore was originally set to join Trump, Navy officials and executives from Anduril, a military technology company.

“If the president of the United States wants to bring the circus into town and tell me that I’m not allowed to speak to the fact that we were the ones that helped bring the deal, then I will let the circus be conducted while I go back to the work of the people,” Moore told reporters Tuesday.

The clash adds to a running feud between Trump and Moore, a rising Democratic figure who has faced persistent speculation about a 2028 presidential bid. The two have sparred over infrastructure repairs, a sewage spill and other issues. Trump this year even revoked Moore’s invitation to a White House governors’ dinner.

A White House official said Moore was invited “as a guest.”

“President Trump is willing to work with anyone to revitalize our manufacturing sector, which is why the White House graciously invited Governor Moore to attend today's event as a guest,” said the official. “It’s unfortunate that the Governor is now making a multi-billion-dollar announcement about himself by throwing a tantrum over a federal initiative that will bring sorely needed jobs back to his state thanks to President Trump.”

The dispute came after Moore, Anduril executives and Trump administration officials conducted two separate briefings for reporters on the project. Moore called it one of the largest economic development projects in Maryland history.

“This is a massive new project that’s going to deliver the largest private investment and create the most jobs in Maryland in well over a decade,” Moore said Monday.

Anduril’s president and chief strategy officer, Chris Brose, speaking before the fight erupted, credited Moore and his administration with helping land the project, calling them “remarkable champions” and saying the state had been “incredibly welcoming.”

The company plans to build a 2-million-square foot shipyard at the former Bethlehem Steel site that is expected to support more than 14,000 jobs.

The Navy has awarded the company a production contract worth up to $2.9 billion for submarine components. Administration officials cast the project as part of Trump’s broader effort to rebuild U.S. shipbuilding capacity and expand the maritime industrial base.

The Navy, which is struggling to increase submarine production, approached Anduril about joining the Virginia-class submarine program. The company then launched a nationwide search for a site for the new facility.

Moore said Maryland moved aggressively once his administration learned about the competition. Maryland and Baltimore County have committed to incentives worth up to 13% of Anduril’s anticipated private investment, plus workforce training.

“We just wanted to make sure that they saw not just our interest and aggression in moving forward, but just showing the uniqueness that Maryland could offer for this being the home for this project,” Moore said.

entries.title: Federal Judge Denies Stars and Stripes Ombudsman's Reinstatement Request
entries.summary: Jacqueline Smith’s case, which alleges the Pentagon violated her First Amendment rights, remains open.
entries.content:
A federal judge denied fired Stars and Stripes ombudsman Jacqueline Smith’s request to be swiftly reinstated to her job in an opinion released Tuesday — but did not outright dismiss her case, which claims her firing was a violation of her First Amendment rights.

The Pentagon fired Smith in April from her position as the military newspaper’s ombudsman, a role charged with safeguarding the paper's independence.

Smith sued the Pentagon earlier this year in U.S. District Court in Washington, claiming retaliation for publishing an opinion piece that criticized Pentagon officials for axing comics from the paper. Another federal judge declined to block the department from firing three other staff members last month.

Judge Amit Mehta denied Smith’s petition for reinstatement, saying her speech as a public employee was only protected while speaking “as a citizen” and not as part of her ombudsman duties.

Mehta declined to dismiss the case outright, questioning whether the same legal precedent that did not protect Smith’s speech while working for the paper would also mean that she “therefore enjoys no First Amendment protection from an adverse employment action.”

The Justice Department’s justification for dismissal relies on an argument that “would mean the First Amendment is but a hollow promise for Stars and Stripes journalists — and perhaps its Ombudsman,” Mehta, a Barack Obama appointee, wrote.

The judge gave the Department of Defense until Oct. 20 to renew its motion to dismiss or respond to Smith’s complaint.

entries.title: Sphere Won’t Guarantee Jobs for Maryland’s Unionized Construction Workers
entries.summary: The Prince George’s County Council shot down proposals to reserve 40% of construction jobs for local unions.
entries.content:
The Sphere entertainment venue planned for Prince George’s County will move forward without guaranteed jobs for unionized construction workers despite calls to require the New York-based developers to employ local unions.

The Sphere National Harbor, planned to be a mini-version of the famed orb-shaped venue in Las Vegas, is projected to generate 4,150 construction jobs, according to Sphere Entertainment Co. But there’s no guarantee any of those positions will go to unionized workers after the Prince George’s County Council on Monday shot down two proposals that would have secured 40% of construction jobs for the project for local unions.

The council approved $215 million in government-issued bonds for the Sphere as part of a financing package to bring the 6,000-seat venue to the banks of the Potomac River. While construction unions are left to their own devices, the council passed an agreement allowing union groups to organize workers at the Sphere once the venue opens.

The Sphere is slowly working its way through government approvals before construction can begin. The county council is slated to take a final vote on the $1.4 billion project at the end of the month. If approved, construction will start next year with the venue planned to open in 2030.

Leaders with the Madison Square Garden Family of Companies, which owns the developers Sphere Entertainment Co., have touted a commitment to unionized labor despite opposing the construction labor agreement. Sphere executive Richard Constable told the Prince George’s County Council last month that the Madision Square Garden Family of Companies are “very union-friendly” and would continue that commitment in Maryland.

The original Sphere in Las Vegas had 97% of construction workers unionized and 45% of its 3,000 current employees are union represented, according to Sphere Entertainment Co. 

Still, Constable said at the council meeting last month he had been “clear” that Sphere Entertainment would not commit to a project labor agreement.

Some council members said they feared pushing to require 40% of construction jobs to go to union-represented workers would have jeopardized the Sphere’s future in Prince George’s County.

“This has been a contentious issue that would have Sphere walk away, and we cannot afford to have Sphere walk away in such an important project,” At-Large council member Wala Blegay said at Monday’s meeting.

County Executive Aisha Braveboy said Monday’s vote to move the financing package forward is a win that will boost the local economy by infusing $67 million in annual tax revenue. She said that is three times more than the combined tax revenue from Six Flags amusement park in Bowie, which closed last year, and Northwest Stadium, which the Commanders are leaving to move back to D.C.

entries.title: Russian Oligarch Says Donald Trump Jr. Has Paid Him Back for Wedding Expenses
entries.summary: Umar Kremlev played down the gift, saying it was “a shared event" and "people blew it out of proportion.”
entries.content:
By Jill Colvin

NEW YORK (AP) — The Russian oligarch who helped bankroll Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding celebration says the president's eldest son has paid back the money.

“Yes, he did,” Umar Kremlev told an International Boxing Association press conference in Istanbul on Tuesday. “He did repay the money I spent on the present.” Still, he said he felt the repayment was unnecessary.

“Frankly speaking, I do not understand why he decided to do so,” he went on. “There are all kinds of events organized by all kinds of people. It is as if I invite you to come and visit my country house. Would you expect me to issue an invoice to them afterward?" Speaking through an interpreter, he said that would be "ridiculous.”

ProPublica, a nonprofit investigative website, reported last month that Kremlev, who has close ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin, “footed the bill for hundreds of thousands of dollars of wedding expenses” when Trump Jr. married socialite Bettina Anderson in the Bahamas in May. That included paying to rent one of two private islands where the three-day party was held.

In a subsequent post on her Instagram page signed by the couple, Bettina Trump wrote that they had been married “surrounded ONLY by our family,” but that Kremlev, head of the boxing association, was a “dear friend” who “very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding.”

President Donald Trump, who did not attend the nuptials, previously defended the arrangement but told reporters that the money would be paid back.

“It’s totally allowed," he said. “But, as I understand it, he paid them back.”

“That’s very common,” he added, “I’ve given wedding parties to numerous people.”

Kremlev, who was recently honored with the Order of Friendship by Putin, also played down the significance, saying the celebration was “a shared event" and "people blew it out of proportion.”

“I mean, why can’t we be friends? We are just friends,” he went on. “We are simply friends and what unites us is love for sports."

The focus on Kremlev comes as Russia remains at war with Ukraine following its invasion in 2022 and as Trump has failed to broker a promised peace deal between the nations.

Trump Jr. has previously been scrutinized over his ties to Russia. During the 2016 campaign, his meeting with a Russian attorney in Trump Tower to discuss potentially incriminating information about his father's then-Democratic opponent was a critical element of investigations into whether the Trump campaign coordinated with Russia to meddle in the election to help Trump win.

entries.title: DOJ Is Recruiting Prosecutors to Monitor Polling Places
entries.summary: The departure from long-standing practice “carries the real risk that election interference and voter intimidation will follow,” a former department official said.
entries.content:
The Justice Department is recruiting criminal prosecutors as part of its expanded election-monitoring effort for the November elections, breaking with a long-standing practice of using only civil attorneys and non-attorney staffers.

While there’s no firm rule against sending prosecutors out to monitor polling places, the DOJ has avoided using them in part over worries their presence could intimidate voters and poll workers, former department officials say.

Several DOJ prosecutors, as well as an FBI agent on a special prosecutorial assignment, have already served as monitors in at least one primary election, visiting polls in Arizona over the summer, according to records shared with The Washington Sun and interviews with local officials.

Justice Department leaders have since called on attorneys and staffers from across the department — including those in its criminal divisions — to work as monitors in November, according to internal emails reviewed by The Sun.

The move is part of a Justice Department effort, announced by Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general who oversees the Civil Rights Division, to send an unprecedented 1,000 monitors to polls across the country on Election Day.

That plan has drawn scrutiny from election administrators, advocates and lawmakers over the department’s push to have monitors examine issues beyond the normal purview of the Civil Rights Division and its Voting Section, which manages the election monitoring program.

Historically, monitors have been deployed to specific election jurisdictions to conduct basic oversight such as checking for bilingual services and wheelchair accessibility at polling places. They may talk discreetly with election officials and interview voters on their way out of polling places, but they are strictly trained not to intervene in the voting process.

Dhillon has said monitors will look for cases of alleged fraud alongside traditional voting rights compliance, and DOJ communications during the primaries indicated that monitors were being deployed to help ensure “ballot security” and “ballot integrity” — matters normally overseen by the department’s criminal sections.

A Justice Department spokesperson confirmed the arrangement in a statement Monday, saying that “department attorneys, including prosecutors, will serve as election monitors, as Department personnel have in many past elections.”

Monitors will not identify themselves as prosecutors and must avoid interfering in the voting process, according to the spokesperson, who added that no FBI personnel are participating in the monitoring program.

“Every monitor has the same role: observe for potential violations of federal law and report concerns to the Department, which the Department will review after Election Day and act where appropriate,” the spokesperson said.

Several former Civil Rights Division officials said DOJ leaders may be recruiting prosecutors because they don’t have enough civil attorneys willing to participate after a barrage of firings and resignations under the Trump administration.

“It’s really possible that this is just about numbers and not some shift in the planned approach,” said one former senior official in the Civil Rights Division who spoke on the condition of anonymity over fear of retaliation. “It’s noteworthy, it’s important, and it’s concerning, but it doesn’t mean that the message to voters is that there’s going to be tons of criminal prosecutors out there monitoring the polls.”

Stacey Young, executive director of the DOJ alumni group Justice Connection and a former longtime attorney with the department, said the purpose of DOJ’s election monitoring was always to “ensure jurisdictions with a history of voting rights violations were following federal civil rights laws.”

“That’s why the election monitoring program was run by the department’s civil rights attorneys who were trained to only observe, and relied on civil attorneys and non-attorney staff, instead of prosecutors who can charge election officials and voters with crimes,” Young said.

“DOJ's deployment of prosecutors as monitors,” she said, “carries the real risk that election interference and voter intimidation will follow.”

Civil attorneys from the nation’s 94 U.S. attorneys’ offices have served as monitors in previous elections. Paralegals, analysts and other support staffers who work directly with prosecutors have also participated in the program.

But a half-dozen former Voting Section officials interviewed by The Sun said they were unaware of any instance in which the department has sent prosecutors to the polls.

Criminal prosecutors “absolutely have not done election monitoring in the past,” said Anna Baldwin, who was a Civil Rights Division attorney focusing on voting issues from 2010 to 2025. “It’s not a criminal investigation.”

Another former Voting Section official said it was a matter of custom not to use prosecutors. “We never did that, because if you introduce yourself to a voter and say, ‘I’m a prosecutor,’ that’s just more intimidating,” the former official said. “Sending prosecutors out would have been less helpful because other people have more relevant experience.”

Over the summer, the presence of a handful of prosecutors monitoring polling places in Arizona didn’t appear to cause any problems.

At least seven criminal prosecutors worked as election monitors in Arizona during the state’s primary in July, alongside several civil attorneys and staffers, according to public records provided to The Sun by the legal advocacy group Democracy Forward.

The prosecutors appear to have all come from the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Arizona, according to the documents. Some went out in Maricopa County, others in Pima County.

One of the prosecutors, Clay Rehrig, is an FBI agent working on a special detail that involves prosecuting violent crimes and hate crimes, according to his LinkedIn profile and news releases from the Justice Department.

Maricopa County’s deputy elections director for communications, Jennifer Liewer, said she was not aware that some of the monitors were prosecutors but emphasized that there was “nothing out of the ordinary” in the way they conducted themselves at polling places.

She said DOJ officials reached out beforehand to let her office know they intended to send monitors, and that once on site they asked for bilingual materials.“They went about it the way they normally do,” Liewer told The Sun. “Maricopa had a very typical experience.”

Things also went smoothly in Pima County, according to Elections Director Constance Hargrove. Monitors there asked poll workers about training and assisting Spanish-speaking voters, she said.

“The visit was no different from any other visits in past elections,” Hargrove said in an email.

A spokesperson for the U.S. attorney’s office didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Several civil attorneys DOJ dispatched as monitors during the primaries have raised alarms among election administrators and voting advocates because of their behavior at polling places or their ties to efforts challenging President Donald Trump’s loss in the 2020 election.

Among them was Joseph Voiland, a new addition to the Civil Rights Division who helped monitor polls in Fairfax County, Virginia, according to public records shared by Democracy Forward. The records were first reported by CNN.

Before joining the department, Voiland served as a lawyer for the Trump campaign in a bid to overturn Wisconsin’s 2020 presidential election results. At least two other civil attorneys who served as monitors previously worked on 2020 election challenges, according to the records.

Across the Civil Rights Division, as The Sun has previously reported, a majority of current attorneys have been hired since Trump took office last year.

Another recent hire to the division, David Levin, pleaded guilty to charges related to his illegal accessing of government election websites in 2016, records show. Levin served as a monitor in Maricopa County, according to the records.

Monitoring during the primaries mostly proceeded without incident, but tensions escalated in Wyoming after officials said monitors there crossed the line.

During the state’s primary in August, Laramie County Clerk Debra Lee said two DOJ monitors asked to examine ballot tabulators and training guides, and wanted to know how new voting equipment was acquired.

Those questions “appeared to me to be outside the scope of federal voting rights laws,” Lee told The Sun in a statement in August. Wyoming’s Republican governor asked the state attorney general to look into the monitors’ actions.

According to public records shared by Democracy Forward, the monitors were John Casali and Jake Bachand, civil attorneys who joined the DOJ recently after working at Trump-aligned nonprofits.

“My advice to my fellow county clerks in Wyoming and to election administrators in other ‘red’ states is don’t think this won’t happen to you,” Lee said in her statement. “Know what the law allows monitors to do and what it does not, and what the monitors’ intentions are.”

entries.title: ‘Enough Is Enough’: DOJ Asks Judge to Shut Down Discovery Motion in Kennedy Center Case
entries.summary: The Justice Department implored a federal judge to “immediately” reject the motion to compel the government to provide communications between Trump and Kennedy Center officials.
entries.content:
The Department of Justice on Tuesday asked a federal judge to reject Rep. Joyce Beatty’s attempt to compel the government to provide documents about President Donald Trump’s role in the Kennedy Center’s planned two-year shutdown.

Government attorneys asserted in a response filed to U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper that Beatty’s discovery request for documents is unnecessary, saying the information already before the court supports the Kennedy Center board’s vote to shutter the center.

“Enough is enough,” the DOJ lawyers wrote. “The Court should not entertain Plaintiff’s and counsel’s efforts to mire this litigation in unnecessary and massively burdensome discovery simply because Plaintiff and her counsel believe something must be wrong with the Board’s well-supported decision to take an action with which Plaintiff, for undefined reasons, evidently disagrees.”

Beatty’s lawyers filed a motion on Monday accusing the Trump administration of improperly shielding evidence behind presidential privilege, saying it “stonewalled discovery” by withholding communications between the president and Kennedy Center officials.

“Absent the Court’s intervention, Defendants will be allowed to curate the record and hide the truth from the Court,” the Ohio Democrat’s legal team wrote.

Government lawyers asked the court to “order discovery closed immediately” and decline to reopen the process if the Oct. 9 discovery deadline passes before the judge can rule on the DOJ’s request.

The attorneys later said the Trump administration had already complied with the “Plaintiff’s requests for information” under a “severely expedited discovery timeline” in the case — and strongly rejected Beatty’s claims that communications revealed in discovery would reveal any misconduct by the Trump administration.

“None of the voluminous evidence provided to her thus far supports her unfounded theories of impropriety,” the DOJ attorneys argued, describing Beatty’s motion as a “desperate efforts to seek additional discovery.”

The Ohio congresswoman, who serves as an ex officio board member, has continued to challenge Trump’s push to reshape the institution since he took control of its board and leadership. The president has said that the iconic D.C. landmark is in a “virtual state of collapse” and asserted that only a complete shutdown of the main building, in addition to a more than $250 million renovation project, can save the performing arts center.

Trump has also taken specific issue with Cooper, a Barack Obama appointee, blocking the addition of his name to the building’s facade under President John F. Kennedy’s name. Trump threatened to halt planned construction for the center after it closed on Sept. 15 unless he is allowed to add his name.

In a Time magazine interview published last week, Trump declined to rule out demolishing the Kennedy Center if his name isn’t added to it, with or without congressional approval.

“I’m not committing to anything,” Trump said.

entries.title: D.C. Closes Anacostia Rec Center Basketball Court Due to HVAC Issues
entries.summary: The recreation center next to Ketcham Elementary School opened in February and cost $16 million to build.
entries.content:
The D.C. Department of Parks and Recreation closed the indoor basketball court at the recently opened Anacostia Recreation Center at Ketcham because incorrect HVAC settings warped the court’s floor.

The department said in an alert Tuesday that it corrected the HVAC issues and is “continuing the required repair, which falls under warranty.” Officials expect to complete the work by mid-November and will keep the court closed until then, according to the alert.

Other parts of the center, which include a fitness center, classroom, multipurpose room and kitchen, remain open to the public while the repairs continue.

The center, initially proposed in 2020, opened to the public in February after construction began in 2023. The project’s budget was $16 million to build the 15,000-square-foot facility next to Ketcham Elementary School.

The facility was intended to provide an indoor gymnasium that the school could use, according to plan documents. Ketcham Elementary is under renovation for the next two school years, and students and staff have been relocated across the street to its designated swing space at 1409 V St. SE.

Jamila White, chairperson of the Ward 8A Advisory Neighborhood Commission, flagged the basketball court’s closure on social media Tuesday morning, asking how a “brand-new $16M facility” closes.

“$16M spent. 6 months open,” White’s post said. “Now the Anacostia Rec Center gym is closed because the floor buckled. It’s been almost a month with no reopening timeline. 30+ young people are outside daily with little to no programming.”

The Department of Parks and Recreation and the Department of General Services referred to the alert when asked to comment. The Parks and Recreation department did not specify when the basketball court was closed.

D.C. Public Schools referred to the Department of Parks and Recreation and the Department of General Services when asked to comment.

entries.title: Is the U.S. Prepared for Another Pandemic? Russia’s Plague Scare Resurfaces Concerns.
entries.summary: The CDC said “there is no evidence suggesting any immediate danger to the US public.”
entries.content:
News of a laboratory worker’s sudden death in Russia from an unidentified infection has public health experts questioning if the United States is ready to handle another pandemic.

President Donald Trump told reporters he has a call scheduled with Russian President Vladimir Putin regarding the plague scare and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said “there is no evidence suggesting any immediate danger to the US public” in a post Tuesday on X. The mysterious circumstances around the death, which has prompted Russian officials to quarantine a reported 200 people, has nevertheless resurfaced concerns around Trump’s handling of the COVID-19 pandemic and the nation’s public health preparedness in its aftermath.

“This administration has really dropped the ball on ‘ancient’ diseases that aren’t supposed to affect us anymore,” said Joseph Allen, a professor of exposure assessment science at Harvard University, citing the measles outbreaks around the country.

The Office of Pandemic Preparedness and Response Policy sat empty for much of Trump’s first year back in office. The White House began restaffing it with a health official and biosecurity specialist this summer — hires that were heralded by the public health community but broadly seen as not enough.

Former officials are not confident that the Trump administration has maintained necessary infrastructure to address another pandemic domestically.

Dr. Ashish Jha, who served as the White House coronavirus response coordinator under President Joe Biden, said that the national stockpile of masks, ventilators and other personal protective equipment was filled by the time he left his role but the country has “to constantly replenish it.”

As the Trump administration has laid off thousands of employees from the CDC, he is not sure that has been the case.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

There are also some signs that the political backlash to COVID-19 restrictions, emboldened by current Republican leadership, could make it harder to manage a large-scale public health crisis.

For instance, Sen. Mike Lee, a Republican from Utah, posted to his personal X account, “I’m not going to wear a mask again,” in response to a post on the death in Russia.

Allen said he does not buy into the assumption that people would not be willing to take COVID-19-like precautions if another pandemic transpired, though he remains concerned that the country isn’t prepared.

“Whatever hits next, and I don’t think it will be this, but we don’t have the systems in place to stop it,” he said.

The World Health Organization has stated that there is a low risk that the disease that killed the lab worker in Russia spreads globally. Initial reports from Russian media said that the woman might have died of pneumonic plague, according to reporting from The Associated Press. Russian authorities, though, have said that the woman died of pneumonia of “unknown origin” that was not connected to her work in the lab at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.

Trump did lend some legitimacy to worries about a potential spread. He told reporters on Monday that the U.S. would help Russia and that pneumonic diseases were harder to treat.

“The microbes and the germs have gotten stronger disproportionately, so we’ll help them,” Trump said.
